In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations can allocate specific time slots for model-based tasks, either in a context-aware setting where context is shared among stations or in a context-free setting. We examine two model allocation scenarios: context-aware TDD, where stations share context, and context-free TDD, where they do not. We develop a non-cooperative game to determine allocation strategies for context-aware and context-free TDD, aiming to minimize interference and ensure reliable communication. Our analysis includes verification of the existence and uniqueness of a Nash Equilibrium in both games, along with an approximate learning algorithm to ensure that the base station's learning context converges to the Nash Equilibrium. We also devise a performance guarantee to measure the impact of model allocation on network throughput in both games. To validate our findings, we present a simulation-based example utilizing a LTE network. Our results demonstrate that, compared to static TDD, context-aware and context-free dynamic TDD can increase throughput by 30% and 25% respectively, and that our proposed algorithm reduces the regret to nearly zero within 300 rounds of play. Our analysis and simulations can be applied to other wireless applications, such as Frequency Division Duplexing. The code for this study is available online at https://github.com/hongseok-lee/ModelAllocation.

In this work, we aim to gain insight into the underlying mechanisms of Hamiltonian Neural Networks by examining whether it is possible to approximate the gradients of a loss function using these networks. We demonstrate that HNNs are capable of estimating the gradients of an arbitrary function, and show that this ability allows them to optimize loss functions through gradient descent. Additionally, we discover that using the estimated gradients in a stochastic optimization process allows us to recover the original loss function, albeit up to a constant factor. Furthermore, we find that HNNs can be trained to estimate the gradients of a specific loss function, from which we can recover the original function by taking the inner product with the parameters. We believe that our results will help shed light on the relationships between Hamiltonian Neural Networks, optimization processes, and the tasks they can perform. We also hope that this work will be the first in a line of research exploring the connections between HNNs, differential games, and optimal control, that could enable the use of these networks to acquire the benefits of different optimization objectives. We have made our code available for public use.

By balancing rating and data contribution activities, participants assign more trust to more accurate predictions and provide additional data where models exhibit the greatest level of inaccuracy. Through mathematical proof and simulation, we demonstrated that the proposed mechanism leads to an equilibrium point where the distribution of trust ratings and additional data contributed by individuals maximizes overall reliability while minimizing costs. By proving that the ratio $(Q_{M_\lambda} - Q_{M_0})/\text{vol}(M_\lambda)$ tends towards zero as $\lambda$ approaches zero, we demonstrate an aspect of the volume hypothesis. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant improvements in WSD tasks, however, the underlying methods lack clear transparency regarding their operations.  In response to this challenge, our research delves into the workings of BERT-based WSD models and associated context-gloss data, highlighting the significance of gloss information in resolving WSD ambiguities.  Our study reveals that gloss information often parallels the context of a target word, sometimes even surpassing its own utility.  In response to this discovery, we propose an integration method that combines context and gloss data for enhanced performance in WSD tasks.  Our proposed method involves incorporating gloss data into the context of a target word by employing a word-injection technique, which we evaluate through a series of experiments conducted on three disparate datasets.  Our findings show that the proposed approach yields consistent performance gains, averaging 10% more accurate results when compared to conventional BERT-based methods.  We open-source our code and associated models at the following link: https://github.com/yueguo1993/Context-Gloss-Enhancement-for-WSD.

This study focuses on key aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance linking, a retrieval task is incorporated into the schema lookup, utilizing a memory bank to store referenced schemas for future value filling reference. To facilitate value filling, a filling task is performed after schema linking, leveraging the stored reference schemas. A unified parser addresses both challenges, yielding a compact design that outperforms competitive baselines. When applied to AMR parsing, it achieves top results across all subtasks, and on the SQLNet dataset, it surpasses the existing record, with a 10-fold decrease in error rate compared to the current benchmark. Additionally, it demonstrates practical utility in a real-world setting, following instructions conveyed through text alone to perform database queries. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/TextSQL. Moreover, a dedicated website hosting interactive demonstrations is available at https://textsql.grua.me/.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory for interacting Bose gases, describing fluctuations in the phase space of both sound waves and condensates. Building upon prior work, we've expanded the model to include correlated fluctuations in both momentum and position. This leads to the introduction of sound wave condensation, resulting from coupled fields that share quantum properties. Furthermore, we've derived precise formulas for key condensate properties, such as momentum, density, and a new quantity called density condensability. These formulas incorporate both macroscopic sound wave fluctuations and relate closely to the ideal case of a perfect gas. We've also investigated non-equilibrium situations, utilizing a 1D hydrodynamic model to describe fluctuations along a directed beam. Our findings match previous research on directed beams within the regime of low heating rate. Additionally, we've explored the relationship between our model and earlier static and dynamic descriptions of fluctuations. This includes connections to the Bogoliubov theory of sound waves, as well as both the linearized Heisenberg equation and Wigner function dynamics. Our model has direct applications to directed beam and toroidal experiments, providing a tool for predicting condensate properties in both cases. We've also considered a 3D model, which leads to predictions for bulk density and density condensability in both directed beam and expansion scenarios. These predictions relate closely to properties of the model, such as sound wave condensation length, and indicate that sound wave condensation may be observable in experiments on interacting Bose gases. We've further analyzed the 3D model by comparing it to the ideal gas case, focusing on the effects of interactions on condensate properties. We've also derived a generalized version of the model, which we believe should apply to interacting Bose gases in any spatial dimension. We've initially applied our model to a situation described by a linear potential, which allowed us to validate the model by matching previous research on interacting Bose fluids. We've then applied the model to a quadratic potential, which is significant because it relates to the behavior of interacting Bose fluids in a parabolic trap. We've also derived an analytical solution for this case, which includes a crucial prediction about the effects of interactions on the healing length and sound wave condensation length. We've further analyzed this situation by investigating the effects of interactions on the density distribution and density condensability in a parabolic trap. Human instructors typically follow a method of teaching that begins with introducing basic information and progresses to more complex topics through trial and error, building on previous knowledge. This approach allows students to learn and remember information more effectively. This text discusses the underlying principles of this approach, describing how students' internal mechanisms process and apply this method to acquire and retain knowledge. We also examine the implications of this framework for various learning issues, such as the retention of misleading information, the acquisition of new versus familiar skills, and the development of explicit versus implicit knowledge. Furthermore, we consider the potential applications of this framework to artificial learning systems and discuss related research in machine learning. We conclude by outlining potential research directions related to teaching artificial systems and exploring the connections between this framework and other related theories.

We also find that the benefits of using BF are more pronounced when the model size is large and the number of possible values per variable is small. Customized web search results page rankings, a common practice by search engines, may lead to users missing pertinent information. Despite its widespread use, research on this phenomenon has been limited, with most studies relying on hypothetical scenarios. In contrast, our study employs a novel approach, leveraging a real-world event as inspiration. During our investigation, we noticed that a particular Google web search results page seemed unusual, with a large block of missing initial results. This page ranked the local listings section at the top, unlike Google's standard customization for our area. We hypothesized that a specific query would yield the typical customized results page. To confirm our hypothesis, we conducted an experiment with 60 test subjects, asking them to review a specific web search results page and identify the listed hair transplant specialists in New York City. Our findings showed that the customized results page led to a significant drop in discovery rates, with an average of 4.3 out of 10 specialists going undetected. Moreover, the number of detected specialists was significantly lower for users with a specific Google account setting, known as the local package setting. In fact, we found that this setting limits the results to only the paid Google My Business listings, neglects other relevant sources, and may result in an estimate of over 200 missing specialists per query. Our study highlights the magnitude of potential overlook and stresses the importance of caution when customizing web search results page rankings. We also advocate for more research on this issue and suggest that search engines provide a way to disable this customization easily. Furthermore, we propose that developers of web search applications create features to simplify the integration of diverse data sources for the sake of discovering more comprehensive results. Last but not least, we offer a simple approach to estimate the amount of overlooked information, which we applied to the case of hair transplant specialists in New York City and found that it yields an estimate of 213 missing specialists per query. We conclude our study by examining the possible reasons for the widespread use of customized web search results page rankings and analyzing its implications for the field of information systems. We also outline potential directions for future research on this topic. We hope that our study will contribute significantly to the development of web search applications and inspire further research on this subject. We intend to continue our investigation by creating a general framework for evaluating customized web search results page rankings. This paper introduces a new testing methodology called Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PPE) for evaluating structured models, and finds that it outperforms the existing paired-permutation testing method. PPE refines the pairing step of paired-permutation testing by minimizing the distance between the permuted statistics of two models under comparison, and this step can be achieved through a variety of methods including using the weighted sum of the vectors in question. Our experiments on random features exchangeability models demonstrate that PPE has a more powerful test statistic than paired-permutation testing, and this leads to an increase in the detection power of the testing method. Furthermore, PPE identifies the optimal method for pairing the testing dataset, and this is related to testing for equality of two distributions using a weighted version of the energy distance. Our research on grouped random effects model reveals that PPE has a more sensitive detection power than paired-permutation testing, especially when the models in question exhibit small degree of grouping. Our study on inverse reinforcement learning exchangeability models shows that PPE has the ability to detect the correct model out of two models with a small difference in quality, while paired-permutation testing is unable to do so. Our analysis on the theoretical properties of the testing procedure under the null hypothesis reveals that the estimated permutation $p$-value is asymptotically normally distributed with a known covariance, and this is related to testing for equality of two distributions using a weighted version of the energy distance. Our research on random features exchangeability models, grouped random effects model, and IRL exchangeability models demonstrates that PPE has a detection power for detecting the true model, and this detection power can be further increased by using a dataset that is over 10 times the baseline requirement. Our analysis on the false positive rate of the testing procedure under the alternative hypothesis reveals that the false positive rate of PPE is less than 10% when the signal to noise ratio is less than 10, and this false positive rate can be further increased by using a dataset that is over 10 times the baseline requirement. Our research on random features exchangeability models, grouped random effects model, and IRL exchangeability models demonstrates that PPE has a linear relationship with the signal to noise ratio, and this ratio can be increased by using a dataset that is over 10 times the baseline requirement. Our analysis on the computational cost of the testing procedure reveals that the computational cost of PPE is directly proportional to the number of permutations, the dimension of the vector in question, and the number of dataset used

The fabric space $WF_n$ was recently introduced as a descriptive tool, capturing the topological characteristics of a manifold of dimension $n$. A key property of $WF_n$ is its construction without using the fundamental group $\pi_1$. In this paper, we explore the connection between fabric spaces and triangulations. Specifically, we establish that the number of distinct triangulations of a manifold is equal to the number of distinct fabric spaces, provided that the fundamental group of the manifold is trivial. However, if the fundamental group of the manifold is non-trivial, then the number of distinct triangulations far exceeds the number of distinct fabric spaces. To support this claim, we examine the number of distinct triangulations for various non-trivial fundamental groups and find that it grows at a rate that can be expressed in terms of specific mathematical functions. Furthermore, we find that the number of distinct triangulations also exceeds the number of distinct fabric spaces by a factor that grows exponentially as the dimension of the manifold increases. The primary evidence for this conclusion is obtained from an analytical expression that represents the number of distinct triangulations as the product of two separate components: the number of distinct fabric spaces and the number of distinct embeddings. Additionally, we determine the specific rate at which the number of distinct triangulations grows as the dimension of the manifold increases. The results presented in this paper were obtained by conducting an exhaustive search of all possible triangulations for manifolds with a fundamental group defined by a single generator that satisfies a specific condition, rather than using an analytical approach. The mathematical functions used to support our claims can be verified through an appropriate generalization of the Riemann's hypothesis, specifically the Fabry-Sarabha hypothesis. The extension of our results to manifolds with a fundamental group defined by multiple generators remains an open problem. The results presented in this paper have physical implications, providing a mathematical framework for understanding the concept of space-time triangulation, specifically for systems that are subject to changes and fluctuations. The paper also discusses the role of geometry in the vacuum space-time triangulation, the relationship between the rate at which the number of triangulations grows and the associated change in dimension, and the possibility of predicting the underlying geometry of a vacuum space-time through the analysis of the associated dimension. The paper concludes by examining the relationship between the number of triangulations and the associated change in dimension, the possibility of predicting the underlying geometry of a vacuum space-time, the role of geometry in the vacuum space-time triangulation, and the physical implications of the results presented.

This research investigates double Higgs production in TeV range $e^+e^-$ colliders using Effective Field Theories, and focuses on the sensitivity to non-standard Higgs interactions. We examine four EFTs that involve Higgs interactions: the Light Higgs Sector, the Heavy Scalar, the Heavy Fermi, and the Chiral Light Higgs sectors. We calculate double Higgs production cross sections in these EFTs at next-to-leading order in QED and QCD, and combine these with detector response simulations to establish minimal detectable values for these interactions at three proposed $e^+e^-$ colliders: the Future Circular $e^+e^-$- collider, the International Linear Collider, and the Compact Linear Collider. We find these cross sections in various kinematic regions, and discuss the responsiveness of double Higgs production to non-standard Higgs interactions, such as Higgs couplings to heavy fermions, Higgs self-coupling, and the light charged Higgs pair coupling, which have significant effects in specific kinematic regions, especially at higher energy levels. Acquiring large datasets for training models is a major obstacle in machine learning applications.  For example, creating a model that can perform 3D scene flow estimation off the grid, without access to labeled data, is a significant challenge.  In response to this issue, researchers have turned to active choice of sparsely labeled training data, selecting areas of the image that could benefit most from additional information.  While this approach has been successful in several computer vision tasks, it has not been tried with 3D scene flow estimation.  In fact, because of the precise requirements of this application, choosing densely labeled data may be necessary.  This paper presents a novel approach, Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-Supervised Scene Flow, that utilizes a two-layer architecture to prioritize the labeling of difficult areas.  It achieves superior results when trained on sparse labels and excellent performance when trained on dense labels, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in self-supervised 3D scene flow estimation.  When compared to a model trained on abundant labeled data, it also achieves comparable performance.  This paper also presents a model that can perform 3D scene flow estimation off the grid, without access to labeled data, and to our knowledge, it sets a new standard in this area.  Code is available at https://github.com/zwang-cse/Adversarial-Metric-Training.

Seismic waveform inversion aims to create high-quality imaging of a medium's properties by analyzing seismic data and wave patterns. However, implementing this method on real-world data proves to be challenging due to the influence of noisy data, the complexity of the target medium, and the significant computational requirements. Many current models struggle with medium property imaging, especially in areas where the propagation of seismic waves is complex, such as in areas with significant subsurface fluid movement. A major issue with these models is the slow speed at which they conduct calculations, necessitating faster algorithms to achieve feasible results. In this study, we introduce a new wave source function that significantly expands the waveform inversion algorithm's capability to handle noisy data while reducing the computational burden. We also introduce a hybrid algorithm that combines two current fast waveform inversion methods to increase the quality of imaging results. To validate this new model, we apply it to a real seismic data set featuring complex fluid movement, and compare it to a current, widely-used waveform inversion method. The results show that the new model's imaging quality is superior to the widely-used method, and it has the additional benefit of being a free open-source tool. In the future, we plan to enhance this model's capability to handle noisier data and to explore its potential applications in electromagnetic wave inversion. This study investigates a two-species voter model on a random network, focusing on the scenario where species interact and compete, and how this affects the dynamics within the model. By analyzing the model's parameters, we identified three possible outcomes for the species' interaction: one species will disappear, the two species coexist, or one species drives the other to extinction. The model shows stability in regions where both species coexist or one species dominates, but it also exhibits a fragile state where it collapses into a state with a single dominating species. In these models, small events, such as the creation or destruction of a connection between a node and the model's exterior environment, can significantly impact the outcome and lead to diverse consequences, including the sudden death of one species or its survival. We created a phase diagram that maps out the possible outcomes for the model, and our analytical findings are supported by numerical simulations. The study demonstrates how the model's topological characteristics, species interaction rules, and environmental factors interact and influence the species' dynamics. The complexity of the model's dynamics is revealed through extensive numerical simulations, and the possible connections to other models, such as the forest-fire model, are also discussed. The study provides a basic framework that can be applied to more complex models, including those that generate self-similar patterns and are characterized by a competition-colonization balance. In experiments involving particle collisions, neutral long-lived particles could escape detection if they interact too weakly with standard matter. A combination of missing energy and specific decay patterns might indicate the presence of these particles. To effectively identify them, it's crucial to understand the characteristics of various decays that involve little or no particle production. This work highlights the potential of Belle II to recognize signatures of which decays produce neutral long-lived particles that could lack detection, focusing on those involving axion-like particles emitted at large angles. By utilizing simulated data and decay processes, we've established that Belle II can easily detect a range of decays featuring low-energy axion-like particles emitted at wide angles and with significant probabilities of occurring. In particular, the experiment can efficiently recognize decays of heavy mesons known as $B$ and $\Upsilon$ mesons into a photon and a axion-like particle, given their considerable likelihood of happening. In optimizing for the detection of these decays, we found that the most effective approach involves analyzing for a single decay process at a time, and that shifting the cutoff for energy thresholds below 2 GeV significantly enhances the identification of these particles in many cases. In total, we've established that Belle II is exceptionally skilled at recognizing a wide range of $B$-meson decays that produce neutral particles with small interactions and can effectively detect all such processes with probabilities of occurrence above 10%. In contrast, the detection of $\Upsilon$ meson decays that produce neutral particles with small interactions is significantly less effective, with only 5.6% of all possible processes with probabilities of occurrence above 10% being identifiable. In general, we recommend analyzing for a wide range of decays involving the creation of axion-like particles with energies above 5 GeV, given their relative frequency of occurrence. In addition, we suggest maintaining relatively narrow angular selections of $\cos(\theta) > 0.8$ when searching for these decays, given the concentrated angular distributions associated with many of them. In conclusion, Belle II has the capability to discover an extensive list of $B$-meson decays that produce neutral particles with small interactions and low momentum, and we present several examples of these decays in the accompanying figures. In the process of identifying these decays, we found that the collaboration can effectively detect all such processes with probabilities of occurrence above 10% for $B$ mesons, and derive concrete numbers for detection efficiencies of specific decays, given their energy thresholds and angular distributions. Language models like BERT have successfully been applied to a variety of tasks involving language, including identifying changes to text, with great results. This study explores the underlying mechanisms of BERT in detecting text modifications, gaining valuable insights into its workings. We discovered that BERT primarily focuses on the context surrounding alleged modifications, considering them less important for analyzing semantic changes. Utilizing this context, we achieved high levels of performance in predicting text modifications, with results showing that BERT's effectiveness is influenced by factors such as sentence structure and semantic distances between original and altered texts. We further demonstrated BERT's effectiveness in distinguishing genuine from fabricated text modifications by developing a detection model that achieves outstanding performance on a variety of evaluation metrics. Ultimately, our analysis and techniques can be applied to a range of tasks involving text, including but not limited to semantic change detection. We hope this study marks a significant advancement in understanding BERT and other contextual language models, paving the way for further innovative applications using these models. We have adapted the path integral formula for coherent state projections in terms of a discrete lattice, suitable for computational analysis using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. As a test case, we utilized this approach to investigate a propagating harmonic oscillator at the quantum level, calculating its average position and momentum. Comparing our results to theoretical predictions, we validated our method and examined the influence of key parameters on the initial propagation equation. Furthermore, we explored two disparate harmonic oscillator scenarios: one with an extremely small beta value affecting propagation, and another with a beta value substantial enough to approach classical behavior. Our-computational method was found to align with both of these cases. Additionally, we obtained approximate expressions for its momentum and position averages in the intermediate beta regime, enabling further understanding. Finally, we discussed the application of our method to a propagating harmonic oscillator to a real-world scenario, such as a particle moving through a medium. Next, we modified the approach to examine a scenario where the harmonic oscillator's amplitude is subject to damping. This involved introducing a novel immunity technique to ensure proper convergence of our Monte Carlo simulations, and we were able to recover known results from both our initial and improved methods. The latter case with damping also sparked our interest as it relates to quantum dissipation, a complex topic that has been difficult to understand and requires additional analysis. We show that any countable collection of homeomorphisms from a surface to itself, preserving boundary components, is precompact with respect to the Roelcke metric. This result extends to collections of mappings that vary within a given boundary component, and we demonstrate its connection to the compactness of certain graphs of measurements. Furthermore, this precompactness holds when considering the space of homeomorphisms that fix specific surface features, such as points, curves, or areas. Our proof utilizes a variant of the Gromov-Félix-Proper compactness theorem for graphs of measurements and the ability to compactify the space of homeomorphisms fixing a surface curve. The contribution of this research is highlighted by contrasting it to the known fact that uncountable collections of surface homeomorphisms are not precompact with respect to the uniform convergence topology. The approach employed in this study also provides a framework for further investigations into the compactness of various surfaces under different homeomorphisms. The findings of this paper further build upon the results established by the authors in their prior work, specifically the article titled "Uncountable collection stability of torus homeomorphisms". The concept of animacy refers to the degree to which entities are living, where higher levels represent greater lifefulness. Previous studies suggest this arrangement is a fundamental aspect of human language, influencing how words are organized in the mental dictionary. However, it is unclear if animacy plays a role in visual processing outside of language, and if so, how it is represented in the brain. In the present study, we examined the structure of the animacy continuum in a visual context using synthetic stimuli featuring shapes with varying features of lifelessness, and tracked the brain activity they elicited in the ventral temporal cortex, a key brain region involved in object recognition. Our findings show that the relationship between shape features and the degree of lifelessness they convey is linear, and that this relationship is reflected in the activity of specific cells in the VTC. Furthermore, a computational model was able to accurately replicate the activity of these cells based solely on the input shapes, demonstrating that the VTC's response to lifelessness can be predicted using a simple learning algorithm. When we modified this model to predict word meanings, its performance declined significantly, indicating that the way lifelessness is arranged in VTC is distinct from the way it is arranged in the mental dictionary. Consequently, our results challenge a commonly held assumption about the organization of the VTC, specifically that its response to objects is ranked along a single dimension of animacy. Rather, our findings suggest that the VTC's response to objects is arranged along multiple dimensions of life, including those related to action, size, and surface, and that the degree of life of a given object is the sum of these dimensions. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, focusing on tasks with partially shared input structures.
A novel approach, unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation, is proposed to achieve this by utilizing unlabeled samples from the target dataset to acquire new knowledge.
This method involves pairing models with relevant existing examples to fine-tune their performance, thereby expanding their expertise in a way that reflects the distribution of the unknown data.
In practice, this is achieved by constructing a diverse set of sampling weights from the target dataset, allowing the model to incorporate the desired changes by weighting the outputs of multiple retrievals.
Experimental evaluations on both text-to-text and classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, surpassing the performance of baseline models and establishing a new benchmark in the area. The rapid spread of COVID-19 globally led to China experiencing a significant surge in digital rumors, which exacerbated challenges in preventing and controlling the virus transmission. To better understand the structure and influence of these rumors, this study leverages a mixture model combining Gaussian mixture model and infinite Gaussian mixture model to analyze messages reported by the Chinese government as well as user-generated content on social media. The study reveals that the majority of questionable information consists of vague posts with limited evidence, and a smaller portion comprises opposing or ambiguous opinions. Furthermore, the study finds that the majority of user-generated content falls into the category of opposing or ambiguous opinions, and a significant portion of digital rumors tends to maintain their validity even after official denial. The study also assesses the impact of digital rumors on the public's anxiety and government trust, and identifies key factors influencing the dissemination of rumors, including media format, source attribution, and the presence of opposing views. The study's findings provide valuable insights for establishing an effective dissemination management strategy and reveal that the presence of opposing views or critical thinking on social media can significantly reduce the influence of rumors on user anxiety and government trust. The study's methodology and findings can be applied to research on the spread of misinformation outside the context of COVID-19. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered, utilizing panoramic scans of planetary nebulae to determine their distances based on population statistics. This method excludes extremely faint nebulae to minimize the impact of foreground interstellar gas and aligns closely with a particular population density model, converting this alignment to a distance through proportional relationships. A comprehensive database of 1350 identified planetary nebulae in the Fornax cluster region has been created, and different researchers independently applied this method to determine the distance to the galaxy cluster, yielding consistent results with a standard deviation of 4.5 percent. This analysis also delves into the characteristics of planetary nebulae populations within the galaxy cluster, revealing a close alignment with the fundamental plane and probing the effects of metallicity and stellar mass. Furthermore, a comparison with other distance measurement methods reveals that the planetary nebulae standard error is minimally affected by metallicity but requires a refinement in its current form to align with other methods. This research was conducted as part of the Fornax3D spectroscopic survey, a comprehensive study of galaxies within the Fornax cluster conducted using integral field spectroscopy and observing the galaxy cluster in various wavelengths, including near-infrared and optical spectra. Integrating continuous queries into streams is efficient with stream processing engines like Lagrange, but these engines struggle with periodic streams that require the same frequency of refresh as the queries they contain. This limitation leads to significant space costs and slow query performance. To address this challenge, we present LifeFlow, a stream processing engine designed specifically for periodic streams. LifeFlow uses a dual-timebase approach, separating timeframes into segments controlled by refresh and execution timelines. This design allows for flexible frequency options and more efficient evaluation approaches. Furthermore, LifeFlow incorporates a focused window management system, reducing memory expenses and accelerating window operations. Compared to Lagrange, LifeFlow demonstrates significant improvements in performance and lower memory usage in tests using periodic streams. Additionally, LifeFlow shows better performance when compared to Lagrange on tasks involving frequent refreshs. The optimal frequency LifeFlow finds for a given application leads to additional memory savings of up to 50% in addition to the already observed 2.5 times reduction in memory costs when compared to Lagrange. Alongside this, LifeFlow's dynamic window approach results in a 22-30% performance gain in tasks involving frequent refreshs. The LifeFlow engine, available under the Apache-2 license, offers pre-built binaries for Windows, Linux, and macOS. The LifeFlow repository, available on GitHub, includes additional information on installing and using LifeFlow. The development of LifeFlow also leads to possible avenues for improving engines targeting streams with variable frequencies. The research behind LifeFlow further suggests possible refinements to the LADR query language specification, particularly in regards to the frequency element within the query definition. Moreover, LifeFlow demonstrates a promising approach to enhancing the efficacy of engines targeting streams with varying refresh intervals, as well as streams with distinct frequency components, without the need for additional speedup or optimization techniques. When applying deep learning models for classification tasks, it is commonly observed that small changes in loss functions result in consistent improvements in performance.  This phenomenon can be interpreted by examining the relationship between loss functions and model performance, considering that it depends on the objective of a loss function, to what extent it is optimized, as well as the unique characteristics of each loss function.  This study investigates how different loss function alteration affects the model's performance, as well as its impact on selected crucial deep learning applications, such as data augmentation, transfer learning, and robust learning.  Our findings can be utilized by researchers and practitioners to understand the impact of loss function alterations and help them make informed decisions about their own tasks.  We also explore the contextualization of loss functions and the idea of personalized loss functions to enhance the performance of deep learning models.  Our research provides a starting point for a novel line of inquiry that could lead to a unified theory of deep learning.  We further examine the concept of transfer learning from a perspective of context transfer, asking whether it is possible to train a single robust deep learning model that can be applied to multiple related tasks.  Our findings show that there are five distinct stages of context transfer, representing challenges that need to be overcome in order to achieve successful transfer learning in practice.  Our study in robust learning against adversarial attacks highlights the connection between the loss function, model complexity, and robustness, leading to the development of a novel robust adversarial training algorithm.  Our research in semi-supervised learning leads to the development of a simple, scalable technique called asymptotic activation mapping, which can be used to compare the effectiveness of different loss functions and provides an estimate of the optimal model complexity.  Our findings in multi-task learning show that there are multiple optimal solutions, and our research in single-task learning is validated by using synthetic data.  Our study in robust learning against noisy labels provides a context of noisy labels as a form of context noise, our research in memory-efficient deep learning provides solutions for reducing memory costs without decreasing the model's performance, which can be achieved by decreasing the model complexity by selecting an appropriate loss function.  Our research in federated learning leads to the development of a novel technique called federated meta-learning, which enables the development of personalized models on a federated platform.  Our study in model compression against compression ratios provides solutions for reducing the model complexity by selecting an appropriate loss function, which can be achieved by decreasing the model complexity without decreasing the model's performance. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge facts represented as if-then statements, which we assemble from the internet and categorize statements by their components including causes, actions, objects, results, and true nature. This comprehensive atlas of common knowledge enables us to create various inference tasks such as identifying cause and effect in statements, determining the primary subject of interest, and categorizing the type of action described. We demonstrate the versatility of ATOMIC by incorporating it into existing natural language processing frameworks, specifically transformer-based models and rule-based systems, which in turn enables us to tackle challenging tasks like distinguishing fact from opinion and identifying implicit causes. With over 140,000 recorded statements, ATOMIC stands out as one of the largest datasets of its kind, offering a wealth of information for developers and researchers working on natural language understanding, specifically within the context of if-then inference, context-dependent inference, and context-neutral knowledge. We publicly release ATOMIC at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Uy4mUevGvHhP1GzGey8XVUWpJH5T1T5M.

The speed and accuracy of quantum linear algebra systems, particularly those using quantum approximate optimization, can significantly benefit various practical applications, as demonstrated by NISQ-HHL. This approach, developed specifically for near-term quantum devices, efficiently provides the imaginary part of linear algebra problems by leveraging hybrid classical-quantum resources. To evaluate the potential of NISQ-HHL, we applied it to asset allocation problems, which involve linear regression, and compared its performance against other quantum alternatives. Our findings show that NISQ-HHL offers a more accurate result with a 68% success rate in comparison to other options, yet it requires significantly longer execution times due to hybrid classical-quantum implementation requirements. Nonetheless, our results also indicate that NISQ-HHL can handle increasingly complex problems as its implementation improves, offering a promising pathway for scaling quantum linear regression to larger-scale applications. Our asset allocation code is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Quantum-Asset-Allocation/NAAA.

To improve the effectiveness of large language models in speech recognition, it is suggested that speech and text be learned in unison. However, learning from two sources at once also presents challenges, including duplication of efforts and the need for balanced weight adjustment. Additionally, existing approaches do not address the issue of asymmetrical data volumes characteristic of speech and text data. To address these issues, a new framework is proposed that simultaneously learns from speech and text through a bidirectional process. In the speech-to-text direction, the model is fine-tuned to generate the expected text output based on an input audio signal, while in the text-to-speech direction, it predicts the audio signal that corresponds to a given input text. To handle the duplication problem, a shared loss function is applied to both directions of the model. To manage data volume asymmetry, a focus mechanism is implemented that concentrates the model's attention on different modalities based on their respective data volumes. To prevent overfitting, a regularizer is introduced that penalizes the model's focus on either modality. Experiments conducted using the Librispeech corpus demonstrate a 5.3% reduction in word error rate compared to a baseline Wav2Text model. The proposed approach also succeeds in transferring learned speech recognition capabilities to a different dataset, the Google Speech Recognition Test. The results indicate that the proposed multi-modal learning framework is effective and can be applied to various speech recognition tasks beyond just the Librispeech corpus. The underlying code has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ghr96/SpeechTextTogether. Measurements of superconducting nanowires can reveal their ability to maintain superconductivity when an electron is injected into the material. In this study, we investigate the conductance of nanoscale niobium nitride wires by controlling the gate voltage to position the Fermi level and thus observe the 2e periodicity of Nornquist effect and the phase shift that indicates the wire's ability to accommodate an extra electron. We explored various wire samples with different sizes and shapes, and in some cases, we observed the phase shift to change suddenly, which could be misinterpreted as Coulomb blockade occurring at a particular gate voltage. However, by analyzing the data in detail, we find that these sudden changes are actually related to the movement of the superconducting gap as we change the gate voltage. The widespread occurrence of these phase shifts in all samples suggests that they are a fundamental property of superconducting nanowires rather than a feature specific to the particular NbN material used in this study. The distribution of the phase shifts can be used to predict the properties of specific wire samples based on their dimensions, which in turn affects how easily extra electrons can be injected into the material. The occurrence of the 2e periodicity of Nornquist effect in some samples is more challenging to explain and may require additional theoretical analysis. The research was conducted using a setup that allows for precise control over the gate voltage and the injection of individual electrons into the nanowires, and the data was analyzed using a model that takes into account the superconducting gap and the distribution of states near the Fermi level. The findings have significant implications for using superconducting nanowires for quantum computations and other applications that rely on the injection of extra electrons into the material. In recent years, video forecasting has gained significant momentum in the self-driving industry to enhance visual perception beyond the present moment. Primary research focuses on predicting short-term future scenes, with most approaches relying on present and historical frame representations to forecast future frames. However, our proposed framework takes a distinct approach by utilizing both current and historical frame representations to predict perspective videos from a single image. This novel method extends the scope of research beyond the limitations of historical frame dependencies and self-driving applications, also offering potential utility in simulated gaming environments. Our proposed model achieves superior performance in perspective video forecasting on multiple datasets, surpassing the standards of both quantitative and qualitative evaluation criteria. Understanding how epidemics spread within densely populated environments like public transportation systems is crucial for developing effective public health strategies. Yet, studying these developments can be made easier by assuming a well-mixed framework, which treats contacts between individuals as random events, even if they occur in a spatially confined setting. Our research involves analyzing two well-studied models within a well-mixed framework and compares our findings to available data on the spread of the SARS virus on a bus in Tokyo. By correlating our simulated results with actual outcomes, we can assess the limitations of a well-mixed framework in predicting the behavior of an urban epidemic. Along the way, we also explore a key issue related to the recovery phase of an epidemic. Ultimately, our simulation enables a controlled examination of a particular bus scenario, allowing us to demonstrate the implications of a well-mixed framework for forecasting disease spread in a crowded bus environment. Along the way, we also derive a specific expression that characterizes the effectiveness of a well-mixed framework in predicting disease spread, which we refer to as the spatial gap parameter. Our results highlight the potential risks of a rapid bus transmission and highlight the importance of accurately determining the level of mixing that occurs in a particular setting in order to predict epidemic outcomes accurately. A linguistic theory known as Centering, which explains how co-reference is organized within sentences and conversations, has been widely applied across various disciplines including linguistics, psychology, and computer science. The theory, incorporating concepts like central entities and side roles, provides a framework for analyzing the co-reference connections within sentences and identifies relationships between them, such as independence and relevance. The centering framework also implies that there's a preference for maintaining the current central entity over shifting to a new one. Developed over three decades ago, the centering theory remained purely descriptive until the introduction of a formal probability model, which enabled the use of computational methods to validate its aspects. Our research involves using neural coreference resolution systems and specifically the BERT-based models introduced in 2020, to re-examine the centering theory through a systematic set of experiments. We developed a new dataset-focused evaluation method that combines precision and a novel metric we call shift score, to assess the coherence of the predicted co-reference relationships within each sentence. Our findings show that the current neural coreference resolution systems effectively identify the central entity by using a specific BERT-based model that prioritizes the highest confidence score, and that these systems prefer the current central entity over shifting to a new one, as predicted by the centering theory. Our research also involves developing a simple neural coreference resolution system that improves the accuracy of the central entity identification by analyzing the sentences and converging to a probabilistic distribution of the centering parameters. We believe our results provide insights into the functioning of the centering theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of neural coreference resolution systems in a way that could guide future research in various disciplines. We are also releasing our code and a new centering-focused evaluation dataset for the benefit of the research community. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/BERT-Centering. In highly elongated polymer chains, flanked by numerous surface bonds on one side, this anomaly allows the ends to occupy a specific region, not covered by the traditional calculation of free energy. This anomaly becomes particularly conspicuous in chain bristles of irregular shapes, where the usual definition of surface areas breaks down. Therefore, a new approach is needed to analyze these complex shapes. By employing a topological analysis of these bristles, we establish the relationship between end regions and other surface features of the chain, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of their free energy costs. This understanding can be applied to arbitrary shaped bristles, allowing for a comparison with irregular shapes that possess molecular-level details. Additionally, this research highlights the significance of distinguishing between surface knots and surface points, as well as the crucial role of looped regions that can encircle the chain's length. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that in elongated bristles, the end regions' cost is directly proportional to the chain's length, equivalent to its curvature in dimensions higher than two. This finding is particularly evident when examining free energy costs of circular bristles through recombination mutations. This research provides an innovative approach to analyzing the free energy costs of polymer bristles through combinatorial methods, offering a fresh perspective on the interconnection between surface points, knots, and looped regions, as well as the role of dimensionality in the proportionality of end regions to the chain's length. This analysis can be applied to a wide range of polymer bristles, including linear chains, circular chains, and bristles with various surface features and complex shapes. By utilizing the PS1-SSP catalog of narrow-band asteroid observations, a method was developed to detect binary asteroids by analyzing the slight orbital deviations caused by the gravitational effect of a companion object. This approach was applied to 43 known binary asteroids whose components are spaced closely enough to cause noticeable effects on their orbital paths. By comparing the predicted shifts in the positions of binary asteroids in photos from the Pan-STARR1 survey, a detection system was created which used a custom machine learning model to identify potential binaries among unclassified asteroids. This resulted in the discovery of 13 new binary asteroids, in addition to 10 previously suspected in studies of the solar system's early formation. Both confirmed and suspected binary asteroids were found to prefer narrow orbital paths, indicating a possible preference for prograde orbits. Furthermore, comparisons with the masses calculated from orbital shifts and those derived from the HCM method revealed differences, suggesting that some asteroids may have slightly elliptical orbits rather than binaries, and highlighting the limitations of the current method, which only analyzes the effects of binary formation and does not account for the influences of resonance or external forces. The most precise mass calculations for 21 binary asteroids also revealed a narrow range of total masses between $10^{17}$ and $5 \times 10^{17} grams$, which may have implications for their formation rather than just being a binary-specific feature. The accurate calculations of mass have been made publicly available on the N-body Workshop website. The code used to detect binary asteroids is available on GitHub. The results from this study, combining the data from the Pan-STARR1 and Sloan surveys, reveals a distinct binary asteroid population in the asteroid belt between spacings of 100 to 300 km, in contrast to the prevailing view that most main belt asteroids are solitary. The discovery of binary asteroids in spacings greater than 300 km is rare, and the occurrence of new small binaries among already recognized binary asteroids suggests that binary formation may continue into later stages of the solar neighborhood's evolution. The findings from this study highlight the limitations of current remote sensing missions in detecting binary asteroids at wider spacings, and the importance of investigating the relationship between binary asteroids and family formation, as well as the surrounding environment, using more detailed analyses of photos and orbital paths. The discovery of binary asteroids in spacings greater than 300 km also provides new opportunities for studying the formation and evolution of small bodies in the solar system, and the results from this study may also be applicable to comets, meteoroids, and planetary moons. Dungeons and Dragons, a renowned fantasy role-playing game, has seen a significant surge in digital adaptations guided by artificial intelligence dungeon masters. These systems use conversations to guide players through immersive stories and challenging puzzles. In response to the growing popularity of D&D, we present a new approach that leverages machine learning to create a highly customizable and flexible digital dungeon master. This architecture comprises two distinct components: a mind that controls the world and a controller that manages the environment. We use intents, a concept drawn from natural language processing, to manage the interaction between the mind and the controller, allowing the dungeon master to easily create and modify scenarios by defining desired outcomes. To accommodate different gameplay styles and player personalities, we introduce a novel mindset framework consisting of multiple overlapping elements that influence how the player experiences the game. By integrating intents and mindset, digital dungeon masters can create rich, personalized stories for players in a fraction of the time required for traditional D&D sessions. We test and evaluate our system on a publicly available D&D dataset, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive toolkit for developing and customizing D&D content, accessible on GitHub. In collaboration with the D&D community, we create a standard mindset framework that players and dungeon masters can use to share and customize games, available on the official D&D website. We also present a standalone command-line interface for interacting with the supervisor, a web-based interface for multiplayer games, and a comprehensive dataset of D&D actions, intentions, and outcomes. In summary, our research offers an open-source, highly adaptable solution for developing digital dungeon masters tailored to individual needs, providing a seamless and immersive D&D experience. In recognition of our contributions, the game's publishers award us the D&D Academic Grant. We discuss potential applications and extensions of our technology, including combining machine learning with traditional D&D content creation methods, developing customizable AI players, and integrating D&D with other interactive storytelling platforms. Last, we outline a future research agenda for the field of artificial intelligence in Dungeons and Dragons.

Our research involves examining the epitaxial growth of Heusler layers on graphene-sapphire substrates and investigates how defects in the substrate influence the resulting crystal structure. We studied a specific Heusler compound, NiFeCr, using a range of techniques including in-situ X-ray diffraction during deposition. Our findings show that the experimentally determined equilibrium between far apart, point-like defects that channel the crystal structure, and the mechanisms of van der Waals and pinhole epitaxy, has never been previously documented. We propose a model that explains the relationship between point-like defects, induced strain, and the peptide sequence of the Heusler layers, and demonstrate how this influence can be managed to achieve perfect epitaxy. Nevertheless, our research reveals that epitaxial growth on graphene-sapphire remains a complex task, and further optimization is required to achieve consistent results. Nonetheless, our study indicates that in certain cases, it may be possible to abandon graphene-sapphire in favor of more conventional oxide substrates, citing the example of nickel ferrite. Our research was conducted using in-situ X-ray diffraction, combined with scanning electron microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and four-circle X-ray diffractometry. Our results have implications for a wide range of research areas, including spintronics, quantum computing, and energy applications. Our study highlights possible modifications to optimize epitaxial growth on graphene-sapphire, as well as alternative Heusler compounds that can be fabricated using this method, including NiCr, NiFeCo, and MnCu, among others. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of generation process, dubbed the $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear construction, which itself utilizes the null space of another code. The rank of a $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code's parameters has been determined, as have the dimensions of its null space, providing an alternative, more comprehensive understanding of these codes. Specifically, the rank of these codes equals the rank of the generator matrix, while the null space's dimension is p^2 times the dimension of the code constructed from it. Notably, two code types arise: those with a specific, simple structure, and those that exhibit no such structure and are thereby equivalent to classical linear codes over the field $\Z_{p^2}$. The former codes possess a particular error-correcting property, while the latter codes fail to demonstrate this property. The study at hand also examines the distribution of the rank of $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, concluding that both code types appear with equal frequency. Furthermore, two $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code ensembles have been proven to be equivalent, a relationship that holds regardless of whether the underlying field is finite or infinite. The research also involves an in-depth analysis of a code construction method, revealing that it is, in fact, a specialized instance of the $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear construction process. The paper at hand closes with an examination of the parameters that define the code construction method, a task that facilitates the recovery of one previously published code construction result. The research further involves an investigation of the error-correcting capability of $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, a capability that exceeds that of its closely related linear code counterpart. The study at hand also involves an investigation of the distribution of the error-correcting capability of $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, a distribution that appears to be concentrated around the error-correcting capability of a related linear code, a concentration that becomes more pronounced as the code's length increases. The paper at hand further involves an investigation of the dimension of the null space of a $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code, a dimension that is p^2 times the dimension of a related code constructed from it.

Multilabel data sets frequently contain instances where a single positive label represents a collection of related labels from a large label space.  If the individual positive labels are used directly to train a multilabel classifier, it will result in multiple incorrect predictions, one for each relevant label.  To compensate for this issue, this paper proposes an method to formally define situations with multiple labeled instances representing the same set of labels, which are referred to as multi-label instances.  A technique is then presented to make use of these instances to improve the performance of a multilabel classifier by creating a more comprehensive training data set that includes precise labels for all instances.  The proposed approach can be time-consuming to compute, so a faster alternative is also provided.  Experiments conducted to evaluate the approach on various multilabel data sets show its effectiveness compared to existing methods.  The proposed approach is capable of handling difficult multilabel data sets, including those derived from text classification data sets where the relationship between labels and instances can be determined based on natural language.  The approach can also be applied to handle situations with multiple labeled instances that represent different labels.  Code for the proposed approach is available at https://github.com/lingeai/ml-instance.  Two possible applications of the approach are discussed in the paper: using individual positive labels that represent multiple labels, and using repeated instances with the same labels to boost the model by increasing the number of training examples.  One potential issue with the approach is that it assumes that all repeated instances have the same label, which can make it less effective when there are instances with different labels.  The approach can be time-consuming and may not be suitable for large-scale data sets.  One possible improvement to the approach could be to make it less expensive to compute by making a single random selection of the repeated instances instead of considering all of them.  This approach can also be combined with other techniques such as ensemble learning, or using a different multilabel classifier, to make it even more effective. The nature of gamma-rays observed in nearby radio galaxies remains unclear, as their powers exceed predictions by several orders of magnitude. In a new study, we examine if disks powered by magnetic captures could be responsible for these excessive gamma-rays. When a fast-moving particle interacts with a magnetic field, it can generate significant heat and light in the form of low-energy photons through electromagnetic interactions. However, the most powerful phenomenon this interaction can produce is the emission of high-energy gamma-rays during magnetic reconnection. We propose that disks powered by captured magnetic energy could shine brightly in gamma-rays and accurately explain the observed gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies. By comparing our model to observations of nearby radio galaxies, we find that disks powered by captured magnetic energy can also explain the excessive hard X-ray emissions and the missing bolometric luminosities in these objects. In the case of nearby radio galaxies with known black hole masses and disk accretion rates, our model suggests that disks powered by captured magnetic energy can shine brightly in gamma-rays, even when the disks are low-density and have slow rotation rates. In a controlled laboratory experiment, we replicated the gamma-ray emissions observed in astrophysical settings by observing high-energy gamma-rays resulting from the interaction between ultra-relativistic particles and magnetic fields in plasma. Additionally, we developed a comprehensive gamma-ray emission model from magnetic reconnection in disks, as well as an analytical expression for the emitted gamma-ray powers, and validated both findings through direct simulation of the interactions. Furthermore, we incorporated our model into a binary evolution code to simulate the gamma-ray emissions from magnetic reconnection in stable, detached accretion disks around black holes and neutron stars, for a wide range of masses and compactness parameters, and found that the beaming corrections for these sources could reach over ten orders of magnitude, resulting in some gamma-ray bright sources being misidentified as they show a dependence on the angular velocity, rather than the spin rate. In a separate analysis, we investigated the relationships between the gamma-ray emissions, the black hole mass, the disk accretion rate, the disk density, and the angular velocity, and found that the gamma-ray emissions are primarily influenced by the density and angular velocity of the disks, rather than the black hole mass or the disk accretion rate, which has important implications for understanding the observed gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies. In a related finding, we discovered a particular stable disk configuration that results in the disappearance of the gamma-ray emissions, which occurs when the disks have sufficient density and slow rotation rates. Diagnosing heart conditions through sound can be challenging due to the variety of backgrounds and body sounds that clinicians must navigate.  In order to simplify this process, machine learning models are being developed to categorize heart sounds with minimal reference to standard recordings. However, these models have limitations when confronted with real-world scenarios, such as the presence of rolling sounds, that can compromise their accuracy. In order to create more practical and reliable models, researchers need to consider the complexities of real-world sounds in their data sets. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that generates more realistic data sets with rolling sounds and background noise that varies naturally, as well as a new technique for preprocessing sounds that are severely distorted, such as those with scarring. When tested against multiple convolutional neural network architectures, this approach demonstrated a significant improvement in identifying heart sounds in real-world settings, with an average increase in accuracy of 7\%. In one of the mentioned cases, the accuracy even doubled from 10\% to 20\%. With simple techniques, such as this paper shows, it is possible to enhance the robustness of machine learning models that categorize heart sounds, thus creating more practical tools for clinical use. In the future, incorporating physiological variability in artificial data sets will likely further improve the efficacy of these models. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and utilizes transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. The code can be used as a starting point for conducting similar research on other healthcare tasks. This paper introduces the concept of "Automated Software Handling" (ASH), a method that enables the seamless integration of multiple software tools into a cohesive system for information processing. As software systems interconnect, they generate numerous opportunities to enhance performance, accelerate development, and boost efficiency. However, this prospect is hindered by the significant obstacle of integrating diverse software platforms, which continues to stifle innovation and limit collaboration. To overcome this challenge, the paper suggests establishing a uniform interface between disparate software elements, thus freeing developers to focus on the core aspects of their applications. The paper also presents an actual implementation of ASH, which combines two renowned programming technologies, Haskell and WebSphere's Enterprise JavaBeans. In this system, Haskell serves as the primary development environment, whereas WebSphere EJBs function as the deployment platform. The paper delves into the specifics of this integration, detailing how it was achieved and the advantages it yields. Furthermore, the paper explores various categorizations of software handling, analyses a non-trivial instance of category transition, and demonstrates how it can be automated. The paper's conclusions are followed by an appendix presenting the source code for the Haskell WebSphere EJBs integration system. The study aims to establish conditions under which a solution exists for a specific variant of this control problem, and to explore the uniqueness of the solution in certain cases. The existence of a unique solution has been established in previous studies for problems without jumping expenses. In contrast, the research presented here considers problems with jumping expenses of a quadratic form, which allows for the derivation of explicit solutions. The study also examines the existence of solutions for two particular cases: one with unbounded jumping expenses and another with jumping expenses that depend on the state. The latter case is further subdivided into two subcases, one with controlled state and another with an independent jumping expense process. The study provides verifiable conditions for the existence of solutions for these two subcases. The cost function in these cases is quadratic, the jumping expense process is stationary and quadratic, and the controller can move or stop moving at any time. To explore the potential of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in confirming the existence of Leptoquarks, we examine the collisions of the two most commonly encountered types, Quark-Lepton pairs made up of a Second-Generation Quark and a Second-Generation Lepton. We calculate the likelihood of these events occurring and analyze the available data from the CERN experiments ATLAS and CMS. The research indicates that even if the LHC energy is increased to 13 TeV, its ability to produce a specific combination of Leptoquark masses is limited. However, if the LHC energy is raised to 14 TeV, it could potentially detect a broader range of Leptoquark masses, with a particular combination of masses at 13 TeV being difficult to identify. The study also reveals that if the LHC detects a specific Scattering pattern associated with Leptoquarks, even if the underlying physics involves two distinct Leptoquark types, it may incorrectly interpret this as being caused by a single Leptoquark type. The research utilizes a comprehensive Leptoquark production software suite and takes into account the various Quark and Gluon collision probabilities that occur during the LHC experiments. The findings are relevant to both the present and future versions of the LHC, and the necessary adjustment factors for calculating Uneven Leptoquark Creation probabilities will be useful for future 13 and 14 TeV LHC experiments, including those at higher energies. The proposed strategy of analyzing Uneven Leptoquark Creation probabilities also offers insights for identifying the specific Leptoquark types that underlie the collision data, particularly in situations where the data is difficult to interpret, as it provides a more precise method of determining the relevant Leptoquark type than the standard mass calculation approach. The proposed method can be applied to future Squark and Doublet Leptoquark types, as well as to the currently studied Single-Component and Uneven Leptoquark Creation cases. The research is consistent with the existing Leptoquark production software results and offers a more detailed and precise understanding of the Uneven Leptoquark Creation probabilities, as well as the necessary adjustment factors for calculating these probabilities. The proposed method can be applied to future LHC energy levels, as well as to the currently studied 13 and 14 TeV cases, and provides a more precise method of identifying the specific Leptoquark types that underlie the collision data, particularly in situations where the data is difficult to interpret.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual merging binary black holes with sufficiently high precision. In fact, current PTA data likely contain signals from such events, which can be recognized by their periodic variations in timing. By employing an accurate approach, our study mimics these signals, taking into consideration the effects of general relativity, gravitational waves, the motion of stars within the binaries, and PTA measurements. In evaluating a specific PTA dataset, our method reveals the presence of a signal likely originating from an eccentric binary black hole merger with a total mass similar to that of supermassive black hole systems. Furthermore, our research indicates that PTA analysts can likely extract more precise information from their data using higher-resolution computational methods. In generating simulated signals, our approach can be quite inefficient, with the computation of a single second's worth of data taking around 80 hours on a standard computer. This, along with other challenges, highlights the limitations of current PTA analysis and the necessity for more advanced computational tools in the study of PTA data. Despite these constraints, the detection of this particular signal remains confident, with an estimated reliability of at least 90%. The methodology we developed for generating these signals has been made publicly accessible to the community. The detection of such signals at other PTA frequencies, with different binary orientations and motion patterns, can be anticipated in the course of further analysis. The found signal's characteristics, along with the detection capabilities of PTA experiments, provide valuable information that can be used in the search for and analysis of similar signals in other PTA datasets, as well as in the study of individual merging binary black hole systems at other frequencies. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address key epidemiological questions. A brief overview is provided of ordinary differential equation (ODE) models, with an emphasis on the transition from basic reproductive ratios to the critical point marking the onset of a sustainable outbreak, as well as the evaluation of intervention strategies through the calculation of the basic reproduction number. Both deterministic ODE models and stochastic infectious disease models have been found effective in epidemiological studies. Although comprehensive individual data are necessary for accurate estimates of transmission rates and other key parameters, such data are often unavailable or poorly quality in many developing world populations. Therefore, other approaches to model outbreak dynamics are also examined, including the use of network analysis, statistical aggregations of individual data, and quasi-experimental designs. A key goal of these models is to evaluate the effectiveness of different control measures, with particular attention to the recent introduction of vaccines in the ongoing pandemic. A strategy is proposed for model selection, as well as a framework for modeling outcomes that go beyond pure epidemiological metrics. Ultimately, a critical perspective on modeling outcomes is presented, with an emphasis on the need for statistical validation of model assumptions and the evaluation of different models against a common standard. A potential research agenda is proposed, with an emphasis on the need for models that combine multiple approaches, the evaluation of different control measures through quasi-experimental designs, and the examination of non-linear outcomes through network analysis. A brief discussion is also provided of the historical contexts of the epidemics examined in this study, with an emphasis on the potential long-term impacts of the ongoing pandemic on ancient and primordial populations.
