A second-order structural control model incorporating changes in permeability is examined to determine its impact on the underlying dynamics. The model features a controlled component represented by a first-order differential equation and an uncontrolled component described by a stochastic differential equation influenced by a random change in permeability. The resulting stochastic process can be reinterpreted as a fractional diffusion process, allowing for the assessment of diffusion complexity in various scenarios. Our study demonstrates that the Nuzzi-Nicolosi arena, a symbolic representation of the space domain, remains a suitable framework for examining the dynamics of the stochastic process. However, due caution is advised when drawing inferences from the results, as the Fokker-Planck equation used in the analysis contains a fractional diffusion equation with non-linear coefficients, implying that the process is likely non-normal. Reinforcement learning models are evaluated based on progress in a limited number of turns to master a challenge, however this short-sighted approach can lead to misleading performance potential, particularly when the model has not reached a perfect level of performance. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative method of endless evaluation, in which the assessment of the model is determined by its capacity to improve over time rather than its ability to achieve optimal results within a confined timeframe. We present an eternal evaluation ecosystem called L2Explorer, which assesses models in an endless environment that mimics numerous critical scenarios, an find that the majority of cutting-edge state-of-the-art methods ultimately achieve a state of perfection. Our findings are accompanied by comprehensive statistics and detailed analysis of each individual challenge. We also provide an endless evaluation task for 25 frequently used benchmarks, allowing other researchers to test their own methods against the standards established in L2Explorer. Our aim with L2Explorer is not focused on discovering novel evaluation metrics, but rather on offering a straightforward, universally applicable solution to the issue of eternal evaluation. Our code is available at github.com/ChangKun/L2Explorer.

Monitoring declarative processes entails tracking processes to ensure they comply with specified constraints. Unlike exploratory settings, where processes can be fully observed, surveillance involves dealing with incomplete process information. Unfortunately, existing solutions fall short, as they either focus exclusively on exploratory scenarios or offer incomplete advice due to limited data. We address this gap by introducing a method that guides process managers to gather data effectively, even in the face of incomplete information, and enforces declarative constraints on processes. Given that process data may be subject to errors, our approach also identifies questionable process aspects. We have implemented our method and conducted experiments to evaluate its performance, showcasing that it compares favorably to the existing state-of-the-art approach. Moreover, our method supports interactive process exploration, as demonstrated by a real-world use case. We have made our implementation available to the public community.

We used HST/ACS observations of five galaxy clusters at z~3 to investigate the development of bulges within calm, uneven stellar disks, specifically in low-mass galaxies (Mstar ≲ 10^9 M sun).  By distinguishing between external mergers and disk instabilities as drivers of bulge formation, we found that even low-mass galaxies in clusters have similar bulge-to-disk ratios (B/D) as more massive counterparts even in the early universe.  This is contrary to predictions made by some theoretical models, which suggested that galaxy bulges primarily formed through internal disk instabilities in the early universe.  Instead, low-mass galaxies in clusters at z~3 are largely similar to their massive counterparts, with 50-70% showing prominent bulges and 30-50% classified as pure disk galaxies.  This phenomenon is likely the result of intense mergers during their formation, which caused significant star creation and subsequent structural alteration.  Therefore, we conclude that bulge formation within calm, uneven stellar disks in the early universe is primarily the result of external mergers rather than internal disk instabilities. The observation of a tropical region on the surface of 61 Vir b, a massive gas giant planet orbiting a G-type star, is intriguingly revealed through high-precision stellar spectral analysis. This observation is unusual because it points to the presence of absorbing gases in the planet's atmosphere, specifically suggesting that the observed angular momentum may not be solely attributed to the planet's rapid rotation but could also be influenced by planetary absorption or an unknown internal differential rotation within the planet. This discovery is significant as it provides further insight into the internal dynamics and chemical composition of the planet, and it also highlights the capabilities of high-resolution spectral analysis in detecting signs of absorption within planetary atmospheres. Furthermore, this finding has implications for the study of gas giant planets similar to 61 Vir b, and it also highlights the possibility that the same phenomenon could be present in other exoplanetary systems. This research is part of a larger project that is examining the surface dynamics of gas giant planets, and it is achieving these results through the integration of multiple observations and techniques, including high-resolution spectral analysis of stellar spectra, atmospheric modeling, and mathematical modeling of the planets' internal dynamics. This study was conducted by a team of researchers from the universities of Wisconsin-Madison, Hawaii at Manoa, and California at Berkeley. Complex systems consisting of multiple interconnected components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling complex systems, their construction and dynamic interpretation remain poorly understood. Our investigation reveals that many of these models comprise unnecessary complex components and can be accurately represented using simple, linear techniques. Furthermore, we discovered that, in contrast to typical time-dependent dynamics, the architecture of these models remains constant over time, being a direct reflection of their underlying structural characteristics. Such insights, obtained through the analysis of random Boolean networks, can be extrapolated to other systems where dynamics and architecture evolve independently. Our study also highlights the risk of misinterpreting complex model behaviors as inherent dynamics as opposed to structural feedback from the environment. In such cases, simpler models that account for this external influence will produce more accurate predictions. Our work paves the way for a more nuanced understanding of graph neural networks and provides a critical perspective on their application in modeling complex, real-world systems. Our research is supplemented by code available online at this link https://github.com/ghpugh/GBN-Analysis.

A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in identifying appropriate therapies to promote brain recovery and prevent further damage. Advanced treatments such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and cell-based therapies have shown promise but their effectiveness depends on accurate targeting of healthy brain areas around cerebral lesions. Since imaging techniques have limitations, we rely on mathematical models to accurately depict the lesions, yet determining the most accurate model parameters is difficult. This study introduces a novel approach to model cerebral lesions using three dimensions, and tests the method against real patient data, showing it accurately predicts lesions and compares it to existing methods, demonstrating its superiority. In recent years, due in large part to the widespread use of multi-channel recording technology, two-channel speech processing has become a significant area of study. It involves processing two recorded signals of the same speech to produce a single, more accurately reconstructed speech signal. In the past, convolutional neural networks have shown significant success in this type of task. However, due to their limited ability to capture temporal information, they have significant limitations. To overcome this challenge, researchers have widely adopted recurrent neural networks, which are capable of capturing long-term dependencies and have achieved notable results. Building on this work, this paper introduces a new dual-path RNN model called DPCRN. It combines the strengths of both convolutional and recurrent networks to capture both short-term and long-term dependencies in two separate channels. The model then fuses the features extracted from these networks to improve speech quality in noisy environments. To demonstrate its effectiveness, DPCRN was tested on the Interspeech 2021 single-channel speech enhancement task and the two-channel speech separation challenge. The results show that DPCRN outperforms existing baselines in both tasks. Moreover, its simplicity is a significant advantage over more complex models. The code for DPCRN has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ghrasoul/DPCRN.

Despite significant advances in deep neural networks, achieving high performance on a wide variety of datasets with a deep network remains Eludious. Despite their sophisticated techniques, current transfer learning methods fall short of fulfilling their full potential. In a world where access to vast amounts of high-quality training data and significant computational resources is not feasible, leveraging an intelligent pre-trained network appears extremely desirable. We introduce an innovative technique called Decision-Transfer, a straightforward framework that enables the utilization of a highly advanced pre-trained network with little need for adjustments, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 12 out of 19 datasets evaluated, and a notable gain in performance on the remaining 7 datasets. We demonstrate that with minimal tweaking, an excellent network can be modified to excel in various areas, including natural language processing, where a pre-trained alexnet was able to surpass the performance of a transformed resnet. We also show that by incorporating additional datasets into the training process, our method can lead to a significant gain in performance of up to 12.4%. We believe this technique can be utilized in a wide range of applications beyond the datasets evaluated in this paper. The code has been made available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Decision-Transfer.

In real-world scenarios, agents often collaborate and learn together, sharing their shared experiences and individual expertise. In this paper, we address the challenge of co-observation learning, where two agents, working together, want to transfer their combined knowledge from one task to another without the need for specialized demonstration protocols. We leverage a mix of max-margin temporary models and memory networks to create a robust framework, allowing the transfer of knowledge between related tasks. Our proposed Co-Observation Learning model (COLE) leverages the unique perspectives of each agent, combining their views to create a unified understanding and generating actions based on this combined perspective. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple co-observation learning scenarios, showing that COLE successfully transfers knowledge between related tasks, outperforming competing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulamai/Co-Observation-Learning.

This paper introduces two novel metrics - the effective error probability dpeff and the overall code failure rate Rcode, which provide a more comprehensive understanding of PAC codes' performance. Unlike traditional error rates, these metrics account for the coding scheme's inherent errors and are applicable to code design and analysis. We demonstrate the utility of these metrics by examining PAC codes under channel errors and offer guidance on suitable code design parameters. Additionally, this analysis leads to a notable discovery - there are coding designs that, when used with noiseless data transmission, result in optimal performance but would incur significant decoding errors when implemented with physical layers that introduce minor threshold excess. To mitigate this issue, these areas with excessive error rates should be targeted for additional research to improve the associated PAC codes. Sectors such as deep space communication, where data transmission occurs at a slow pace, and dense block diagonalizing DPC links, which involve complex, time-consuming decoding processes, may benefit from this discovery. To further contribute to the community, this work's findings and conclusions are presented in the form of a graph that can be used by researchers designing new PAC codes. To date, various research papers have investigated PAC codes for specific applications, but few have analyzed the code's performance itself rather than its effectiveness when implemented. Notable examples include papers by Geist et al., Belfanti et al., and Liang et al., which explored specific scenarios and identified potential errors in the code's failure rate. On the other hand, researchers typically evaluate coding scheme performance using simulation-based testing, which is time-consuming and less practical for rapid data transmission. To address this issue, this paper proposes and presents a simple, analytical method for calculating the code's failure rate, which can be used in conjunction with simulation-based testing to ensure the code's performance is thoroughly evaluated. To illustrate the practical application of this method, we use the proposed framework to analyze and optimize a specific coding design, namely the Viterbi decoding algorithm, and make the associated code available to the research community. Lastly, this paper clarifies the relationship between the Viterbi algorithm's error probability and the underlying channel errors, which is essential for understanding and evaluating the algorithm's performance. To facilitate this analysis, we derive an expression for the Viterbi algorithm's error probability in terms of the underlying channel errors, which provides a more comprehensive and precise characterization of the algorithm's performance. Evaluating the best action space size for reinforcement learning-based neural machine translation remains unclear, as both discrete word-level and action-probability-based methods have their own strengths and limitations. To address this issue, we investigate reinforcement learning with extensive action spaces of up to 32,000 words and demonstrate that larger action spaces significantly improve the accuracy of selection compared to traditional methods, such as top-k, without experiencing a significant increase in exploration time. To mitigate the challenge of directly applying the exployer-exploiter technique in continuous action spaces, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes the action distribution to define two distinct sets of actions for the explorer and the exploiter, leading to a substantial improvement in translation accuracy with simple hyperparameter adjustments. Our proposed method, along with detailed experimental evaluations on multiple datasets, presents a rigorous examination of action space size's impact on action selection and suggests appropriate scales for practical applications. To further increase translation accuracy, we explore the use of intermediate action spaces to sequence two reinforcement learning processes, with promising results showing a 0.54 improvement in BLEU score on the en-fr dataset. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/ghrua/ReinforceTranslate.

transactions are successful. However, available research focuses primarily on
validating data conditions in MongoDB's transactions, while concurrency conditions
remain unexplored. In response to this challenge, we have developed a tool

aspects: first, validating concurrency conditions is difficult due to MongoDB's

conditions. Consequently, to tackle these issues, our tool validates both data

Our innovative approach combines concealed geometry and differential geometry to create an advanced framework for analyzing complex systems with interconnecting networks. This theoretical structure is applied to a specific magnetic nanoassemblies model characterized by triangle-based interactions, which experience a phase transition as temperature decreases. Our in-depth analysis into the dynamics of this model reveals intricate topological properties, known as singular links, that play a crucial role in the geodesic flow within its phase space. The discovery of a critical temperature where the geometry shifts from hyperbolic to Euclidean geometry marks another key finding in this study. Below this critical temperature, the system's geometry becomes perfectly regular, which contributes to the degradation of the magnetic field's stability. This theoretical analysis predicts the effects of the geometry's shifting characteristics on the dynamics of the system, which includes the destruction of the triangle-based interactions, magnetic field-induced chaos, and the assembly's breakdown into individual components. Consequently, this study demonstrates that despite its intricate nature, the dynamics of network assemblies can be understood through concealed geometry, which provides a more unified and comprehensive analysis of these complex systems. Additionally, this approach offers novel insights into the importance of considering the geometry of space when studying the interactions within these assemblies. This framework's versatility extends beyond magnetic nanoassemblies to similar systems, which can be represented by networks consisting of singular links, and also sheds light on similar phenomena in biological systems, such as the recruitment of immune cells in response to infections. Finally, this study introduces the concept of concealed geometry in systems with interconnecting networks to experts in related fields, with the aim of stimulating new ideas and facilitating collaboration among these communities. We investigated the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere using data from the Solar Probe Plus mission. By analyzing more than 36 million solar wind speed measurements, we calculated the solar wind energy flux for various lengths of solar wind particle paths and compared it to the solar wind speed in those areas. Our analysis revealed that the energy flux of solar wind accelerates at higher rates near the Sun, specifically in regions where the solar wind speed reaches 600 km/s, and that this rate decreases as we move further away from the Sun. Furthermore, we found that the energy flux of solar wind slows down in areas farther from the Sun than the solar wind particle paths would suggest, indicating that the solar wind is still being influenced by its source region. These findings support the theory that the solar wind is accelerated and slowed down across a narrow region near the Sun and provide insights into the energy flux of solar wind in the inner heliosphere. Moreover, we found that the energy flux of solar wind is greater at lower solar wind speeds and that this relationship varies over time. Additionally, we found that the energy flux of solar wind is similar in different solar wind particle paths that originate from the same solar wind speed area, indicating that the energy flux of solar wind is determined by its source region rather than the solar wind particle paths themselves. These results have significant implications for the models of solar wind acceleration and slowing down and highlight the importance of probing the solar wind source regions and the outer surface of the sun to gain a deeper understanding of the energy flow of solar wind in the inner heliosphere. Moreover, these findings provide insight into the energy balance of the sun and the inner heliosphere, which is influenced by the energy gained by the solar wind and the energy lost in the form of solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Finally, these results highlight the significance of the Solar Probe Plus mission in gaining a deeper understanding of the energy flow of solar wind in the inner heliosphere and the importance of continuing and enhancing this type of mission to gain a deeper understanding of the energy balance of the sun and the inner heliosphere. In particular, we observe a significant improvement of 7.3% in the F1-score when adapting to a new environment and a 12.4% improvement when adapting to a new speaker. In practical terms, this translates to systems that are 13 times and 20 times more likely to choose the correct emotion when adapting to a new speaker or environment, respectively. In this research, we delve into the mechanics of linguistic models, specifically pre-trained language models, to better understand their capabilities in arranging words into meaningful phrases. Our investigation focuses on the BART model, a neural summarization technology based on a masked language learning approach. Through the use of modification and deletion experiments, we demonstrate that BART's ability to arrange words relies heavily on their functional properties, above the level of individual words. These functions, which underpin the structure of phrases, are revealed through the analysis of corrected arrangements produced by BART after our interventions. One key aspect evident in our results is that the relationship between words, described as their semantic relations, plays a crucial role in driving the BART generator. Furthermore, our research shows that linguistic models like BART tend to prefer syntactic structures characterized by a high level of complexity, albeit sometimes inaccurately. One interesting aspect observed in our results is that the evaluation of semantic coherence, which measures the coherence of phrases produced by BART, often correlates with the degree of syntactic correctness. In the process of exploring the mechanisms of linguistic models, we also discovered that the evaluation of semantic coherence can be employed to assess the capability of these models to grasp the underlying syntax of phrases. One such example is presented in our paper, where the evaluation of semantic coherence is used to investigate the capacity of BART to recognize the syntactic structure of questions. Our results demonstrate that the capability of BART to arrange words into questions is indistinguishable from its capability to arrange them into statements, based on the evaluation of semantic coherence. However, when we employ an alternative metric called the syntactic accuracy, which evaluates the correctness of the syntactic structure of phrases produced by BART, it reveals a subtle difference between the capability of BART to arrange words into questions and those into statements. One implication of our findings for natural language generation systems based on linguistic models is the importance of incorporating elements that evaluate the capability of these systems to grasp the underlying syntax of phrases, in addition to coherent semantic relationships, in order to ensure their accuracy in producing syntactically correct phrases. One such example is presented in our paper, where the incorporation of an element that evaluates the capability of BART to recognize the syntactic structure of questions leads to a generation system that arranges words into questions with a higher level of syntactic correctness compared to those generated without it. The rapid dissemination of deepfake media poses a significant challenge to information authenticity and spreads false information that can influence public opinion and cause harm to individuals. As such, developing an effective deepfake detection method for various media types is crucial. Presently, deepfake detection techniques primarily rely on artificial neural networks and have shown promising results in various settings. However, various factors such as the continuously evolving deepfake techniques, the need for frequent model updates, as well as the need for highly advanced computational equipment to enable real-time detection capabilities are major limitations of these methods. In this paper, a novel framework called the MD-CSDNetwork is proposed, which addresses these challenges by implementing a multi-domain, cross-trained network for enhanced deepfake detection with significant performance boosts in multiple metrics. Compared to existing methods, the proposed network demonstrates superior performance in multiple settings, as evidenced by our experimental findings. Moreover, this network facilitates efficient in-field deployment by reducing the required training data to a mere 200 images, thereby enabling seamless adaptation to novel deepfake techniques and simplifying real-world deployment. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ygyu1997/MD-CSDNetwork.

In the context of angle functions between subspaces of a given metric space,  Menger raised two significant problems in 1940. The first, posing as a question, inquires about the truth of the statement that in a metric space with an angle function, the subspaces that result from taking the fixed points of that function in relation to a fixed element of the space are closed. The second problem, presented as a conjecture, explores the relationship between this statement and the consistency of a specific set of inequalities. Utilizing the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and its consequences, this study provides solutions to both problems. The conventional approach using the inequality yields the conjectured relationship, while an novel derivation based on the exponentiated angle function reveals the condition of subspace closure. The study further elaborates on the term "metric space with an angle function" by offering a variation that could be useful in specific applications. The research also cites connections to earlier works, including results associated with the Riesz divergence and the Leibniz rule. The author additionally provides two additional solutions to Menger's problems, one involving a specific example and the other a general case, both derived from varying the angle function. The paper concludes by examining the relationship between these solutions and the original problems, as well as exploring potential connections to the recent paper by Birkner, Goldstein, and Moseman on random trees. The results presented in this study have been previously published in the journal Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems, volume 42. We introduce a novel concept - cluster structures for algebraic structures, and demonstrate that the dual space of a quantum group possesses a rich cluster architecture. This is shown to be equivalent to the set of characters inhabiting a specific Weyl chamber, equipped with a particular ordering. As a result, we gain insight into the properties and behavior of algebraic elements, including the development of combinatorial formulas for calculations and the discovery of specific polynomial properties in certain contexts. Furthermore, we find that the cluster arrangement associated with the algebra C(n) is straightforward, whereas the associated fan for A(n) and B(n) forms a well-known polytope, specifically a root polytope. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive description of the cluster change transition, which enables the conversion from the algebraic basis to the character basis, and vice versa. In the process, we establish a connection between the quantum group and a sublattice of the root system, revealing that the latter contains the set of characters defined by the cluster pieces. Finally, we establish that the character basis is constitutively invariant under the braid group action, and that the cluster change transition can be reinterpreted as a result of the braid group action on the character basis, resulting in the formation of the fundamental domain located within the Weyl chamber. This leads to the discovery of distinct character types, including non-regular types for A(n) and B(n), which have not been previously reported. This research was initially presented at the "Cluster algebras and geometric combinatorics" conference held in Shanghai, June 20-24, 2016. The explosive growth of decentralized applications on blockchain technology has enabled new types of schemes like pyramidal scams to flourish. These scams leverage automated contract interactions to appear decentralized and operate beneath the radar of traditional law enforcement. As a result, there's a lack of understanding regarding the structure and strategies these scams employ. This research examines the structure of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scam, from a game theoretical perspective. By analyzing its mechanism, we find that it fits within the category of controlled assets in a moral hazard model, and this structure is beneficial for ensuring participant trust and paving the way for scammer profits. Furthermore, by reviewing transaction data, we reveal that the scam operates by exploiting naive, newly arrived participants who contribute most of their assets, while the majority go on to act as sellers of these assets to other participants. This is made possible due to the fixed daily withdrawal amount that allows them to buy and hold assets from others. This in turn facilitates a steady stream of payments to early participants who were initial contributors. This information is made visible through an examination of transaction data which maps out the flow of assets among participants. This research is an attempt to contribute to the limited body of research on blockchain-based scams. It also demonstrates the use of simple, actionable data from the Ethereum blockchain, and the potential benefits of analyzing decentralized financial transactions. This in turn could be applied to other contexts such as identifying money laundering activity. This research presents the structure of Forsage as a specific example, however this structure is general and other scams could possibly adopt a similar form. This research poses potential questions for law enforcement agencies on how they can detect and prosecute scams of this nature, and for academics on how they can extend this research to other contexts such as money laundering, or on the long term consequences of participating in scams of this type. While this concept has been theoretically plausible for a long time, all previous studies have assumed that interstellar pollen or microorganisms would maintain their integrity and viability upon arrival in a planetary atmosphere. However, in reality, any biological material would likely undergo significant stress, exposure, and genetic mutation during its journey to planet Earth. Therefore, the likelihood of discovering viable extraterrestrial life would depend heavily on how resistant it is to various forms of radiation, cosmic particles, and the extreme conditions it would encounter en route to termination. In this work, we examine the viable existence time of microorganisms in the interstellar medium, incorporating interactions with high-energy radiation, cosmic rays, and meteoroid impacts, and exploring various astronomical settings that may influence their survival. As expected, our results show that the lifespan of these microorganisms is quite short, ranging from 10 to 100 years, although there may be some protective forms like asteroid-based life that could potentially survive for millions of years. Consequently, any detected life forms in the interstellar medium are unlikely to be self-sustaining and instead are likely to be linked to terrestrial life, originating from planetary transfer. In addition, we find that the probability of discovering viable life in the interstellar medium is extremely low, essentially negligible, and that any detected life in space would likely be linked to various forms of bioplastic debris that can thrive even without life itself. In the process, we also discuss the potential misinterpretation of ancient meteoritic organic compounds as interstellar life, highlighting the importance of proper dating and the critical role of cosmic radiation in modifying these compounds. Finally, this research highlights the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the effects of high-energy radiation on astrophysical settings and the viable existence time of microorganisms in these environments. In the process, we also explore the potential of bioplastic debris on asteroids as long-lived indicators of past life, offering a promising avenue for future life detection missions. Animal population studies often aim to understand how animals interact with their environment and select habitats.  Traditional methods of analyzing capture-recapture data primarily focus on quantifying population size.  However, such data contain individual identification information, allowing researchers to combine capture-recapture analysis with resource choice analysis, which can reveal important insights into an animal's habitat selection behavior. We present a capture-recapture analysis method using spatial trap arrays that accounts for both individual detection probabilities and spatial habitat selection among traps.  We also explore capture-recapture analysis using trap arrays in relation to environmental variables, such as elevation, by treating it as a random effect to enhance the generalizability of results to other locations.  To demonstrate this method's applicability, we analyze data from a study featuring capture-recapture data with habitat selection among trap arrays in relation to elevation in a mountainous area.  Our capture-recapture analysis model initially assesses detection probabilities in each trap array while considering individual-specific detection probabilities.  We then model habitat selection among trap arrays as being influenced by a gradient in elevation.  Our results indicate that this method effectively infers habitat selection among trap arrays, as we observe strong concordance between the elevation at which individuals were previously captured and their preference for higher or lower elevations.  We also find that this method can provide more precise estimates of population size than models ignoring detection probabilities. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems focused primarily on detecting lower and upper body movements, respectively. However, there's a growing interest in restoring ambulation specifically, given the high level of autonomy required for safe and efficient walking. This paper's key contribution is re-defining this method's optimization problem to make the analysis feasible for deep neural networks, and demonstrating the efficacy of this variant, named Deep Dynamic EGC, through comprehensive trials on artificial and real-world data. The results show that Deep Dynamic EGC outperforms the base version and other state-of-the-art methods in predicting missing values and identifying crucial connections in time-series data. Moreover, the code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub, presenting a starting point for further modifications and improvements to the approach. The proposed algorithm can be applied to a wide range of tasks including data imputation, feature selection, and classification using the code available online. The code has also been successfully utilized in a climate-based prediction task known as the NAO index prediction. The code's efficacy in predicting the NAO index has been verified through a comparison with other reliable methods including ProxAL, L1L2DCA, and L1DCA, showing a significant improvement of 13% in the prediction of the NAO index compared to these methods. The proposed algorithm can be trained end-to-end using a simple deep learning approach, allowing it to be applied to a wide range of tasks including neuroscience, finance, climate study, genomics, and other domains involving complex system analysis. The code's scalability has been verified through a comparison of the algorithm's computational complexity on artifical data, presenting a linear relationship between the number of samples and the computation time. Due to the importance of understanding these interactions, it is necessary to analyze videos of dogs in motion. This paper presents a method for automatically detecting movement in videos featuring dogs and distinguishes between different types of movement - large movements referred to as "significant movement" and small movements referred to as "natural behavior". The method for detecting movement and behavior utilizes a combination of statistical and dynamic parameters including average speed, speed variance, and acceleration variance.  The proposed approach is applied to videos of dogs and the results demonstrate that it effectively distinguishes between natural behavior and smaller movements, enabling the extraction of more relevant movement information.  The method can be implemented in various applications involving dogs and it is necessary to note that this work can be extended to analyze videos featuring other animals in motion. A concise overview of the approach's fundamentals is provided for inexperienced readers. A notable finding shows that although GPU performance benefits originate from matrix inversion, the acceleration is particularly effective when combining order techniques with GPU-capable matrix inversion tools, especially in the context of Bayesian inference. A simple Bayesian inference example serves as a proof of concept, utilizing GPU-capable matrix inversion from the OpenTMB library. A discussion on the potential issues of overfitting due to increased model complexity is also presented. A simple regularization technique is introduced to address this challenge. A comparison with a purely vectorized implementation using a CPU-capable matrix inversion tool from the Eigen library in a Bayesian inference context on a NVIDIA A100 GPU reveals the advantages of the proposed approach. The proposed approach outperforms the Eigen-based implementation by approximately 4.5 times in terms of computation time. The expansion of the approach is explored to demonstrate the appropriateness of order techniques for complex, real-world problems that can be adapted to GPU computing. The code for the examples is provided as Open Source. We discovered that certain types of random perturbations grant a material topological properties, allowing it to maintain immunity to disorder. A hypothetical "Topological Anderson Conductor" has been proposed, comprising of two coupled two-dimensional layers, with one layer containing random potential perturbations. Our study focuses on this concept and discusses our findings regarding its topological properties. We were able to analyze the topological effects of random perturbations by plotting topological maps for different types of perturbations, and by performing numerical simulations to examine the spatial distribution of electrons in a "Topological Anderson Conductor". We explore a decentralized learning problem in a linear bandit model, where agents are situated in non-identical contexts and make individual decisions. Unlike existing research, we assume that the contexts are unknown and must be inferred. To achieve optimal performance, we develop a decentralized scheme based on least-squares estimation of context and arm parameters. This leads to a minimal order of $n^{1/2} \log^2 T$ regret when the number of context dimensions is small, surpassing the current benchmark for decentralized learning. In addition, this research investigates the difficulty of learning in a linear bandit model and incorporates it into a new variant of the UCB algorithm, which is universally applicable. The integrity of both algorithms is confirmed through theoretical regret bounds, and the effectiveness of the techniques is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the paper. The main challenge of learning in a linear bandit model is also found to grow polynomially with the number of arms, which is an novel observation. The paper concludes by identifying a lower bound on the minimal order of regret in a decentralized linear bandit setting, which serves as an improvement over a previously established lower bound. Our study utilizes Event Shape Engineering (ESE) with central Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy to extract information about the initial state conditions. Two types of event shapes are analyzed: one set of shapes exhibits a long-range correlation pattern resembling elliptic flow, while another set shows negligible dependence on the collision plane. By comparing fitted distributions for both types of shapes, we find their average values follow opposite trends when arranging events by a specific order of multiplicity. Combining this information with hydrodynamic simulations, we determine the initial state condition properties, and verify that the observed patterns are consistent with assumptions about initial state conditions that influence the medium uniformly. Alternatively, we propose a method to investigate the local structure of the initial state by matching events to a fixed level of elliptic flow, rather than arranging events by multiplicity. This approach is compared to ESE, and both methods exhibit the same underlying physics, albeit with different sensitivity to initial state conditions. Lastly, we outline potential applications of ESE for future collisions, including the study of initial state conditions, and investigate the influence of transverse momentum cuts on measured distributions, finding that such cuts primarily influence distributions that characterize the initial state condition's magnitude, rather than its orientation. This work investigates the extremal values of the generalization degrees of freedom (GDoF) benefit that accrues to optimal power control versus binary power control in interference networks with an increasing number of users. We first establish the extremal GDoF benefits for a fixed number of users and demonstrate that it extends to the square root of K with the correct constant, i.e., $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$, by developing a type of reverse Sanov theorem that identifies the extremal points of the entropy function's image under random matrix convolution. Next, we determine the extremal GDoF benefits over time in cognitive networks with an increasing number of primary users, from 2 to any integer, and show that these benefits also scale as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Lastly, we provide a more broad GDoF characterization for both networks. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. The findings presented in this study were previously known, yet the original approach of their derivation remains novel. The study in question was conducted without knowledge of the existing results in [21,22]. The study also introduced two new types of random process inequalities, one of which, the convex combination of time-evolving matrices, may be useful to other researchers. The other, the convex combination of matrix-valued functions, could be useful to the research community at large. This study introduces a novel integration approach for coupling fluid dynamics with particle collisions. The proposed method accommodates variable collision durations and is optimized for simulations featuring a wide range of collision times, including both instantaneous and prolonged interactions. A statistical analysis of particle collisions was conducted to better understand the factors influencing collision durations and their variability. A notable observation was that even in turbulent flows, collisions between particles typically last for a few time steps, often in the range of 5-20 steps for the presented cases. A key feature of the new integration method is that it allows the free flight duration to be determined by collision time steps rather than overall time steps, providing a more flexible framework for simulations. This article presents an innovative approach to achieving whole number solutions for the diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, a more challenging variant of the well-known and historically significant Euler and Pell equations. By applying a factorization technique, we transform the equation into a form that involves an Euler equation, enabling whole number solutions to be found when $n$ is an even number. For odd numbers, we develop a another strategy to determine all possible integer pairs $(a,b)$ for a given $n$, provided that the absolute value of $a$ does not exceed $\sqrt{7^{n+1}}$. A comprehensive list of solution sets for odd numbers is presented in the form of a table. In the process, we also derive a key inequality with an "infinite growth rate" that contrasts with the typically observed "exponential growth rate" in similar problems. The approach used here also offers an alternative, less complicated proof of a previously known result for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ when $n$ is an even number. The article concludes by examining the approach used and its potential applications to more intricate equations, specifically the general form $a^2+ab+b^2=X^n$ where $X$ is a prime number other than $2$. The case for even numbers is well represented in existing literature, but the article also provides a novel solution to the problem of finding all possible integer pairs $(a,b)$ for a given $n$ when $n$ is an odd number. The article offers two such solutions, one complex and one simple, to this problem. The simple solution is similar to the approach used in the famous Euler equation proof by Leveque, but it offers a key distinction in that it uses an infinite growth rate instead of an exponential growth rate, a criterion that is required for its own purposes but could also provide a new tool for other problems. A significant issue in legged robot locomotion is the uncertainty that arises when navigating through diverse terrain conditions. This research focuses on simulating and improving a single-legged jumping robot as it moves over different types of soft terrain, particularly soft balls, while aiming to clear a horizontal barrier. The robot in question is equipped with a hydraulic actuation system and was initially tested on firm ground before being simulated on soft terrain through various testing protocols. Although real-world data is limited, our estimated parameters for the simulation are based on experimental fluid dynamics and hydraulic measurements. Our simulation tool, developed using SimMechs, accurately replicates the robot's dynamics and hydraulic systems and was utilized to explore different jumping techniques on soft terrain. A Komodo multi-physics simulation was also employed to simulate the interaction between the robot and the soft balls, providing crucial information on the stress distribution, deformation, and boundary between hard and soft terrain. Based on the insights gained from real-world jumps and simulation results, a series of controlled tests were conducted to further refine the robot's performance. Specifically, the aim was to increase the height jumped over soft terrain by modifying the footplate, changing the jumping technique, and analyzing the stress experienced by the feetplates. Our findings show that jumping technique has a significant impact on stress experienced, with a 30% reduction in stress achieved through a modified technique. Furthermore, by increasing the footplate thickness, we successfully demonstrated a 20% increase in height jumped over soft terrain. The research was conducted by a single individual, with some external guidance, and was carried out in the Robotics and Mechatronics Engineering Department at Islamic University of Technology. The simulation tools, models, and data are available for download at the website https://github.com/abedalkhair/wiki/wiki/Monopod-simulation. The research was supported by the Islamic University of Technology. The findings have been published in the Journal of Intelligent Robotics Systems [1]. The current version of the simulation includes some limitations and there are several areas for future improvement such as adding surface deformation to the simulation, developing a hybrid controller for the robot, and integrating the simulation with MATLAB environment. The research was carried out in accordance with the laws and regulations of Islamic University of Technology. The research was conducted fairly and honestly, without any deception. The data collected from real-world jumps and simulation results will be used to develop a predictive model for predicting height jumped over soft terrain. In complex information systems, evaluating priorities often depends on multi-criteria decision-making methods that assess values within a hierarchical framework. While various meta-heuristics optimize individual criteria, they typically fail to capture the inherent structure of these hierarchies. This research introduces an expansion model to guide optimization within a hierarchical setting, representing each level as a subset of the lower level by means of assignment and ranking problems. This model can be applied to decision-making scenarios using methods like AHP, ANP, and their hybrid variations. However, its primary advantage lies in capturing the hierarchical relationships, which are often disregarded in traditional optimization approaches. This expansion model provides a flexible framework for incorporating diverse hierarchy definitions, varying from the simple to the complex, and can be implemented using a hybrid genetic algorithm. This study also explores relationships between hierarchies and offers a novel approach to define them using operations on individual criteria. In addition, it presents a set of decision-making guidelines based on the expanded model, including a real-world application in evaluating university rankings. This research can be used by practitioners and academics alike, offering a versatile hierarchy expansion model for information systems and a novel approach to defining interlevel relationships via set-theoretic operations, which can be employed in conjunction with the expansion model to provide a robust and adaptable framework for complex decision-making scenarios. This model can also be utilized as a standalone tool to capture hierarchical structures and has been successfully implemented in a real-world scenario involving the assessment and ranking of universities. It is worth noting that this research has been conducted independently without any connection to the existing works cited. This paper can be viewed as a starting point for further collaboration and integration with the existing literature. However, even when conditions are met, some research has shown that quantum fluctuations can still cause re-traps during the process. This study focuses on investigating the phenomenon of re-traps during quantum quench dynamics. By applying the quantum annealing algorithm to solve N-ORC, the researchers obtained the re-trap probability as a function of closing speed. This information enables exploration of re-trap behavior at various closing speeds, ultimately identifying an optimal interval for effective quantum annealing. Additionally, comparing classical and quantum annealing re-trap probabilities reveals that the quantum annealing re-trap probability follows a power law, whereas the classical annealing re-trap probability follows an exponential law. This study also discovered that the quantum annealing re-trap probability can be influenced by various parameters, including temperature, coherence time, and qubit tolerance. This information is crucial for benchmarking quantum hardware and developing practical applications of quantum annealing. A key finding of this research is that despite generating re-traps, quantum annealing sometimes leads to optimal solutions in the re-trap region. This discovery encourages further exploration of quantum quench dynamics in the re-trap region in search of solution improvements. This study provides a novel approach to investigating quantum annealing re-traps, which can be an effective way to extract quantitative information from quantum hardware. This approach can be applicable to other combinatorial optimization problems. The research was conducted using a 56-qubit quantum processor, specifically the D-Wave Quantum Annealer, although the developed methodology can be suitable for other annealing processors. The study found that the re-trap probability depends on the closing speed, suggesting that the condition for effective quantum annealing, i.e. the re-trap probability being zero, should be met cautiously. The study also found that the coherence time is the most critical parameter affecting the re-trap probability in the Ising Hamiltonian, particularly in the precise cover problem, which is a highly constrained optimization problem. This research provides a novel insight into quench dynamics, specifically the phenomenon of free flow in the context of quantum annealing. The study found that the appearance of free flow is associated with the onset of thermal instability, which marks the boundary within which quantum annealing is an efficient method. The study also found that the fraction of free flow is directly related to the fraction of correct solutions, which can be influenced by various parameters, including temperature, coherence time, and qubit tolerance. We introduce a dual-band model consisting of localized $d_{\phi}$-orbitals at the $x$-site and $d_{\sigma}$-orbitals at the $y$-site to examine screening in infinite-layer nickelate. The $d_{\phi}$-orbitals screen the $t_{2g}$-electron interaction, while the $d_{\sigma}$-orbitals do not. By adjusting the onsite energy difference between $y$-site electrons, we investigate how the band filling affects screening and find that the electron-filled $y$-site band leads to a more pronounced crossovers from the Kondo lattice to the Kondo gas regime, allowing for a possible comparison with experimental findings. However, an infinite layered structure is considered in this study, which might not accurately reflect the strongly coupled nature of the $t_{2g}$-electrons in (001)-oriented nickelate materials. A more appropriate model, taking into account the $x$-oriented geometry, would involve screening by both $t_{2g}$-electron types, potentially leading to a more direct connection with experimental data. Nonetheless, this dual-band model serves as a useful starting point for understanding the role of screening in (010)-oriented nickelate materials, which exhibit the Kondo-disordered regime with a mix of localized and itinerant $t_{2g}$-electrons. This model can also be applied to other materials with $d$-orbital screening in mind. Moreover, we highlight the importance of screening in (010)-oriented nickelate materials and the (010)-oriented geometry in (001)-oriented materials, which may have far-reaching implications for experimental and theoretical studies of infinite-layer nickelate materials. The dual-band model allows for a comparison with the four-band model introduced earlier, providing a more elementary and intuitive understanding of the physical phenomena observed in these materials. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that a harmonic function that remains constant across a specific subdomain of the manifold cannot be identically zero. This result extends the principles of Liouville's theorem and forms the basis for a novel comparison argument, thereby ensuring the equality of two specific manifolds with comparable volumes and constant scalar curvatures. Consequently, one manifold must be a scalar multiple of the other, which in the case of a compact, closed manifold is implied by the well-known theorem of Gao and Li regarding its constant scalar curvature. Alternatively, this result can also be derived from the recent, established theorem of Brendle and Marques. Both of these results have been achieved through the application of Liouville's theorem to harmonic functions, which have a key consequence of their own. This research has been conducted in collaboration with P. Li. The fundamental theorem has been specifically designed to accommodate a broad range of manifolds, as evidenced by its application to the compact, closed manifolds mentioned above, which, as noted before, can also be validated using the established, and more complex, approach of Hamilton's compactness theorem for the class of manifolds with constant scalar curvature. The utilization of Liouville's theorem has been demonstrated through its application in a comparison argument to the Euclidean space, which in turn yields the celebrated Albano-Bartnik lemma, and also in the investigation of certain singular manifolds, specifically those with isolated singularities and minimal energy, which can be validated using the application of harmonic functions. The research concludes by highlighting the potential utility of this result, which could be further expanded upon in future investigations. In recent years, point set processing capabilities have been incorporated into neural networks, enabling the automatic inclusion of new data points without network retraining. However, establishing methods to dynamically add or remove input points throughout processing stages remains unexploited. To address this, we introduce a novel module called a dynamic entrance, which can be easily integrated into neural networks by other researchers. This module employs a gateway that allows point sets to be continually updated, and we find that incorporating a global mean pooling layer within the gateway enhances performance. Specifically, we demonstrate the value of dynamic entrances by incorporating them into a neural network used for 3D object classification, and also showcase their applicability in other point set processing tasks. The resulting code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenXudong1989/DE-RGCN. Moreover, we outline possible future research avenues in this unexploited domain.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are subject to corrections resulting from deviations in general relativity. A key factor influencing this correction is the PPN $\gamma$ value, which measures the gravitational influence on light and has been conclusively determined as 1.00 by the Gaia spacecraft with unparalleled precision. Previously, this value was undetermined and could have anywhere in the range of -1 to 1, requiring its consideration in mathematical models of astronomy. This study analyzes the effect of this uncertainty on parallax measurements, a key component of astronomical calculations, and demonstrates how it results in a Gaia-like measurement system overestimating the distances of stars by a quantity proportional to their mass and luminosity. Additionally, this study determines the threshold above which the effect on parallax measurements becomes significant, and identifies a particular population of stars susceptible to this measurement error. A simple algorithm has been developed to calculate the correction for this error in the calculations of astronomy, and this study recommends determining the PPN $\gamma$ value to a high degree of precision in future astronomical measurements. A possible value of 1.004 has been proposed as a potential variation of the PPN $\gamma$ value that could be tested by future astronomical measurements. To create more realistic chatbots, our model aims to incorporate a feature called semantic connections between questions and answers, which refers to the idea that there's often a relationship between questions that share similar content. In this context, if a question with an unknown answer surfaces that's semantically connected to a previously answered question, the answer to the new question might also be the corresponding answer to the previous one. To enhance the capability of generating semantically connected pairs of questions and answers, we introduce a two-stage framework called Coarse-to-Careful. First, our model generates a broad inventory of possible answers based on a shallow analysis of the question, followed by a more meticulous examination to pinpoint the correct answer. To incorporate semantic connections, we establish an edge between questions and answers that share similar content. To evaluate our approach, we design a novel metric called the connection score, which measures the frequency with which two questions that are connected to the same answer are also semantically related. In this version, we achieve results that rank us among the top three for both natural language processing tasks involved. To further improve our model, we incorporate a feature called self-connected awareness, which enables it to recognize when two questions have a strong connection to the same answer simply because they were asked in close proximity to each other. To implement this, we add an indicator called the awareness score, which represents how closely linked two questions are based on their position within the text. To validate this feature, we create a text-based scenario that mimics real-life conversations and both a human evaluator and an automated tool verify that our model's performance improves in this context. To push our model to the next level, we develop a more challenging version of the semantics-connected question-answering task that involves determining which answer corresponds to which question among three possible questions, given that two of the questions are semantically connected to the same answer. In this version, we achieve results that rank us among the top two for both natural language processing tasks involved. Finally, to apply our model to a broader range of real-life scenarios, we demonstrate that it's possible to modify our framework to focus on other features called semantic connections, which refers to the idea that there's often a relationship between questions that share similar content, by developing two new versions of the semantics-connected question-answering task that involve determining whether two questions are semantically connected to the same answer based on a text snippet, and identifying the answer that corresponds to a question that is semantically connected to one of two possible questions. A systematic investigation has been conducted to analyze the existing spectral data of composite molecular cations containing oxygen. Our research reviewed a broad range of theoretical spectra available online, utilizing multiple search engines and databases, and found approximately 270 relevant spectra, primarily of cometary origin, from various observational campaigns including the Rosetta mission. Although these spectra hold considerable value, some deficiencies were identified, including limited coverage of certain frequency ranges, incomplete data for certain molecules, and limited access to original research papers despite the presence of numerous published studies on the subject matter. Despite these knowledge gaps, the collected data were still found to be sufficiently useful for developing models of cometary spectra originating from Mars and Venus, based on molecular cations. This research highlights the potential utility of the existing theoretical spectra, if researchers make their data more accessible, and points to need for further observations covering the MIIP and HIIP spectral regions. The current state of available data has been made publicly accessible via the APODISK repository for the benefit of the scientific community. The approach employed in this research could also be useful for tackling similar issues related to planetary ring systems, astrophysical phenomena, and spacecraft environments. The proliferation of machine learning techniques beyond the laboratory has been impeded due to insufficient access to large, unified training data. This issue remains prevalent in federal learning settings, where institutions with varying interests, located around the globe, manage sensitive and diverse data. Although significant advances have been made in overcoming data heterogeneity, the federal learning approach falls short in addressing the challenge of highly disparate data. Current methods tend to favor the larger datasets and ignore the significance of smaller datasets, thus compromising their utility. Our research presents a novel random stroll method in the domain of federated learning from diverse data. In this approach, data samples are chosen independently from each dataset for model updates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by implementing it in both symmetric and asymmetric data scenarios. The results show that the random stroll method yields comparable performance to the adaptive method, while successfully leveraging the unique characteristics of smaller datasets. The methodology proves particularly valuable for situations where the underlying relationships between the datasets are complex and difficult to model. The code for the random stroll method has been made available online. Research examining the link between mental health treatment and reentry into the criminal justice system typically relies on self-reported data, potentially skewed by factors such as stigma and fear of punishment. This study addresses this limitation by analyzing the effect of mandatory mental health treatment on recidivism among incarcerated individuals within the Thai criminal justice system. Thai law requires defendants found guilty of certain crimes to receive mental health treatment as part of their sentence. This study compares the recidivism rates of individuals subject to this treatment with those who were not, drawing data from a large and comprehensive dataset containing information on approximately 4,000 offenders sentenced to treatment and over 13,000 eligible comparison subjects. The analysis controls for various factors, including the type and severity of the crime, age, and prior convictions, to ensure a fair comparison. The results show that offenders required to receive treatment had a 7-8 percent lower chance of committing a new crime within three years of release. Furthermore, an examination of court and prison records reveals that treatment is associated with improved mental health outcomes, including reduced suicide rates and lower levels of psychiatric symptoms. The study also explores the relationship between treatment and different mental health components, discovering that it reduces suicidal ideation, anxiety, and depression but has no significant impact on personality disorders, substance dependence, or psychotic symptoms. The research suggests that making mental health treatment mandatory can lead to lower recidivism rates, although it cannot guarantee improved psychological well-being due to limitations in measuring this outcome accurately. The findings hold value for criminal justice systems and incarceration policies elsewhere, particularly in low-and middle-income countries with limited resources. The study indicates that even basic, compulsory mental health treatment can reduce the negative consequences of personality disorders, substance dependence, and psychotic symptoms, although these outcomes vary by category of disorder. A vast amount of medical images is categorized into different types and researchers often need specific subsets for training and testing. Though exchanging medical data is regulated due to privacy concerns, exchanging image categories is unrestricted. To enhance the efficiency of semi-supervised healthcare image segmentation, we propose a new technique that forces consistent mappings between a limited number of labeled images and a large amount of unclassified images. This technique simply relies on maximizing the overlap between segmentation results and uses consistent mapping to tackle exchangeability. We evaluate our proposed method on datasets containing medical images of various types and find it outperforms existing semi-supervised techniques. Moreover, our proposed method allows for continuous learning and we demonstrate its effectiveness in scenarios where data availability changes. Our proposed technique is versatile and can be combined with existing techniques to enhance the accuracy of healthcare image segmentation. Our code is available for public use.

Complex dynamical systems, especially chaotic ones, exhibit unpredictable behavior in their individual components, yet predictable patterns emerge when considering the system as a whole. In this research, a novel graph neural network named CHAOSNet is presented, capable of quantifying chaos within such systems by generating a metric that reflects the system's overall complexity. This metric is represented as a compact time series in one dimension that provides a clear, integrated understanding of the system's dynamic changes and can be utilized for effective classification of different system behaviors. To validate CHAOSNet, it was applied to three distinct systems: the Lorenz system, a real-world hydrology example, and the logistic map. These experiments demonstrated that CHAOSNet effectively distinguishes between chaotic and non-chaotic systems, offers a more accurate estimate of the Lyapunov exponent, and significantly outperforms traditional machine learning models in all cases. Moreover, CHAOSNet was found to be highly interpretable, with its learned features aligning closely with established measures of chaos. The code for CHAOSNet is available at https://github.com/Jeffrey-F/CHAOSNet.

In the analysis of blends made up of multiple substances, it's common to assess the mean and variance of parameters relative to spectral information. This holds true in the context of chromatography, including both GC and LC methods. The maximum likelihood estimation for a first-order normal distribution model assumes independence between the parameters of individual substances and requires a non-negative and precise amount of sample material for each substance. However, in certain situations, such as when dealing with complex samples resulting from the aggregation of multiple similar substances, or when the amount of sample material is insufficient, this approach may break down. This study provides a framework for assessing the mean and variance of blends using Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimation with a non-parametric approach, which can accommodate dependent parameters and is robust to the presence of unresolved substances. The applications of this method to assess the accuracy of measurement tools, such as chromatography instruments, and to determine the concentration of complex substances like petroleum are highlighted. The development of a software tool called PMGL is also mentioned, which implements this method and is suitable for users without advanced statistical knowledge. The results show that the Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimation method leads to accurate assessments of the concentration of complex substances, even in situations where a significant number of substances remain unresolved. The availability of PMGL software allows users to easily access this method and other assessment tools through a user-friendly interface. The development of this software also provides users with the source code, allowing them to customize and modify it to suit their needs. The integration of PMGL with popular chromatography data analysis software like AMDIS, URDAMDIS, and NIST IDEAS provides a seamless measurement analysis tool for users of these programs. The results of this study are relevant to researchers and scientists who use chromatography to measure the concentration of complex substances and can be applied to other measurement techniques, such as mass spectrometry. PyKT is an open-source Python library designed to simplify testing and comparison of knowledge tracing models that utilize deep learning. This framework provides accessible functions to evaluate existing models, compare their performance, and test new methods for estimating student abilities. PyKT also supports the use of multiple processes to quickly execute time-consuming tests, such as those involving multiple students and multiple model combinations, and facilitates the creation of customizable reports to present evaluation results in a clear and organized manner. With its user-friendly features and extensive functionality, PyKT aims to streamline the development process for knowledge tracing models and related research by minimizing the overhead of testing and allowing users to focus on modeling and data preparation. Version 1.0 of PyKT includes support for evaluating models using multiple students, multiple initial observations, and multiple attributes, and is capable of executing tasks quickly by utilizing multiple processes and storing temporary data in memory. This version represents a significant improvement over the initial prototype presented at the ACM Conference on Emering Technologies for Computing, Learning, and Teaching in 2020. This version of PyKT includes 12 demonstrated tests and models, and is available under the BSD-3 License on GitHub at the url https://github.com/ktresearch/pykt.

Creating effective proof systems for SMT solvers involves a delicate balance in designing a format that is both convenient for users and soluble for verifiers. A simple proof format might easily lead to user convenience but may lack efficiency in solving, as seen in theories like floating-point arithmetic. In extension theories, where additional functions are incorporated into a base theory, proof generation can be particularly challenging. Our proposal, a new proof format called Universal SMT Proof Format (USPFF), aims to accommodate diverse extension theories by providing user-friendly commands while incorporating solving strategies from verifiers. The USPFF framework is versatile and allows for user customization through configurable modules that can be tailored to specific application needs. Our evidence format has been implemented and is available for public use through the Alethe platform, which also offers a module for verifying floating-point arithmetic proofs. Our future plans involve refining the USPFF format and expanding the Alethe solver to handle additional proof formats. The USPFF format and the Alethe solver can be downloaded from https://alethe.github.io/.

This paper introduces two innovations to enhance the efficiency of federated learning with synchronous aggregation. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across languages with different character sets. In this paper, we introduce a new ASR transfer approach, incorporating a two-step decoding process that first obtains a rough text output, which is then converted into a more detailed version. We apply and modify this approach for Russian-to-English ASR transfer and also explore encoding and decoding options to enhance its performance. Our experiments reveal encoding the target dataset in a form similar to the source dataset leads to significant improvements in WER (13.49% to 10.17% for zero-shot and 12.67% to 9.35% for fully-supervised transcription respectively). Moreover, using a more advanced encoder and decoder leads to an additional WER reduction of 5.53% for zero-shot transfer and 3.08% for fully-supervised transfer. Our findings are particularly notable for zero-shot transfer where we achieve a 13.49% WER. Our code is available at github.com/aleksandar-eric, this repository includes all necessary details for replication.

Research in navigation systems for marine robots focuses on combining internal sensors with external signals like radio frequency (RF) transmissions, satellite connections, or combinations of these, to determine their position and orientation. Since these systems are subject to motion-related errors and external influences, filtering techniques like the Kalman filter are commonly employed to provide accurate estimates. This paper introduces a novel navigation system based on Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), which accounts for sparsity and the variability of data to improve estimation accuracy. We introduce a new GPR model to describe the sparsity of observations and the variability of data to derive a narrow state transition matrix, which reduces the impact of prediction errors. We also derive an adaptive method to determine the sparsity parameter and the noise level for the GPR model, which enhances estimation accuracy by addressing changes in environment visibility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this navigation system via simulations and real-world experiments. In one simulation, we showed that this system's performance can be up to 99.87% better than existing GPR-based navigation systems when the environment changes slowly. In another simulation, we found that this system's adaptive method can increase the accuracy of estimates to 95.63% when there are sudden changes in the environment. In real-world experiments, we found that this system's performance can be up to 99.87% better than existing GPR-based navigation systems when the environment changes slowly. We also found that this system's adaptive method can increase the accuracy of estimates to 95.63% when there are sudden changes in the environment. We demonstrated the variability learning filter's ability to adapt to different scenarios, including scenarios with fast changes, partial occlusion, and indoor and outdoor environments. This research can be applied to navigation systems for marine robots in various environments, including underwater rivers, tunnels, and indoor and outdoor spaces, as well as to other state estimation applications in other fields. This leads to the development of a partial differential equation system representing the conservation of energy-momentum and vorticity for each fluid component. Our analysis also considers the scenario where there are multiple interface curves separating the fluids from each other and from vacuum space-time. In this case, we derive conditions for asymptotic stability regarding the partial differential equation system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these conditions are met when the interface curves consist of a closed surface without contact points. This leads to the recovery of results on the asymptotic stability of spherical fluids in General Relativity, as well as the outcome for multiple fluid systems in the parabolic case. Our approach is applied to a broad class of fluids, including perfect fluids, Einstein-Manabe metrics, and the Chern-Simons complex scalar field system.
