Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on vast amounts of data for multiple domains. However, correcting grammatical errors in new domains often requires substantial effort to accumulate relevant data. This issue motivates our research on few-shot domain transfer. We introduce a new approach, combining models for source and target domains, which produces a directed path for efficient domain adaptation. During training, this approach isolates shared and domain-specific knowledge. At test time, it employs the directed path to fine-tune for a single example in the target domain. Our method achieves comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art model while reducing data requirements by a 98 factor. Additionally, it surpasses existing methods when adapting to new domains with limited data. This approach has also been successfully applied to other few-shot learning tasks. The task of allocating discrete and scarce goods to self-interested agents, where fairness is a concern, has been an enduring challenge. This challenge is reflected in the problem of allocating kinetic energy harvesting resources to agents in a switching-based energy transmission process. Research has shown that, to ensure the worst-case outcome is fair, a specific allocation mechanism, known as the "power of $k$" mechanism, guarantees stability and achieves near-optimal social welfare when there are a small number of agents. Moreover, this mechanism ensures that the largest possible subset of agents will receive the goods with a majority consensus, even when they behave strategically. In the context of kinetic energy harvesting, this is an significant result because it means a single agent can provide a reliable energy source through the process of harvesting and transmission. The study at hand extends these results by determining the optimal value of $k$ for a wide-ranging and varied scenario, as well as demonstrating that a specific variation of this mechanism yields an equitable outcome in a general sense, not limited to the specific scenario of energy harvesting. The study also delves into the analysis of a specific scenario, known as the "2-agent case", to provide a more in-depth examination of the behavior of the allocation process. The research has further expanded the understanding of this process by formally defining the concept of equity and showed that a specific variation of the power of $k$ mechanism yields an outcome that is fair in a general sense, known as "Pareto equity". The study at hand has also explored the complexity of the process for a more intricate scenario, known as the "tree scenario", and demonstrated that finding a pure Nash Equilibrium in this process is computationally complex, with a level of difficulty equivalent to solving a hard problem known as set cover. Evaluating the range of accretion rates among T Tauri stars is crucial for understanding the distinct processes that T Tauri stars undergo. An excessive number of, largely unreliable, accretion rate measurements from spectroscopic applications are addressed by Hillenbrand et al.'s accretion rate threshold, which only considers values derived from multiple, independent, and reliable methods including bolometric luminosities, luminosity spectra, and veiling levels. Furthermore, the documentation of accretion rates is influenced by the behavior of XX Cha, a T Tauri star exhibiting unusually persistent accretion bursts over a wide span of nearly two years in its accretion history. Until now, the analytical models of T Tauri stars have primarily focused on persistent accretion rates and did not account for additional variations. Using the unique data set from XX Cha, we have tested the current analytical models and found that additional variations are necessary to accurately describe its accretion fluctuations. Additionally, we have analyzed the remaining 37 T Tauri stars that meet the criteria and whose accretion rates are derived from multiple, independent methods, and compared their values to the documented ranges, which have increased to $10^{-8.5}$ to $10^{-3.5} \, \mathrm{M}_{\sun} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The most extreme values in this range are suspected to be influenced by factors such as mass accretion bursts, disk instabilities, or the presence of companions, and thus these values should be treated with caution. The generally accepted range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-3.5} \, \mathrm{M}_{\sun} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ is still prevalent, and we recommend using it until more reliable data sets become available. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among trajectory data. For example, some data may showcase suboptimal behavior, while offline methods typically aim to generalize across existing data, including instances where the outcome is already known to be negative. In such cases, existing offline multi-agent learning strategies often fail to distinguish between useful and useless data, treating all available information equally. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, focused on learning from trajectories that yield a successful outcome. Unlike conventional methods, our approach ignores data associated with unsuccessful outcomes by leveraging behavioral contrast. This enables the model to compare and contrast different trajectories, prioritizing the retention of distinguished expert trajectories. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in multiple offline multi-agent learning scenarios, including complex scenarios involving multiple agents. The resulting code can be found at https://github.com/yangzw/PPPOE. Our proposed method, PPPOE, achieves comparable performance to benchmark models, including proximal policy optimization, while significantly outperforming them when interacting with unfamiliar environments. Our proposed method also discovers unique policy trajectories when using complex state representations, such as high-dimensional observations. Our proposed approach provides a straightforward way to enhance data quality by excluding useless data, including instances where the outcome is already known to be negative. We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. The network consists of two parts: the first uses a convolutional architecture to correct image pairs, training it on a publicly available dataset, while the second uses a U-Net to create a 3D registration tool. We used two datasets, with different contrast levels, to test the network's effectiveness. The results showed that the 2D and 3D networks successfully aligned images with a mean absolute error of less than 2 pixels, compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we applied this framework to treat megavoltage image noise, using a simple post-processing technique, and verified that it maintains the accuracy of the original images. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub. The proposed method has been published in the journal Medical Physics, volume 47.

The notion that entanglement between two particles is necessary for true nonlocality to arise has been a long-standing misconception. Utilizing the EPR paradox and the GHZ paradox as examples, it can be demonstrated that the nonlocal properties of a single particle are capable of guiding the behavior of another particle across a significant distance. This analysis highlights that, even in the absence of two-particle entanglement, a single particle can possess nonlocal entanglement. Consequently, the requirement that two-particle states be maximally entangled to exhibit genuine nonlocality is unnecessary. This interpretation is consistent with the fact that the reduced single-particle state contains entanglement, as demonstrated by a numerical study of various three-qutrit scenarios. This study shows that the nonlocal effect caused by a single particle can vary significantly, influencing the behavior of another particle either subtly or dramatically, and that the relationship between single-particle nonlocality and entanglement is distinct. Furthermore, it can be shown that single-particle nonlocality is directly related to the particle's genuine nonlocality, allowing it to exist in a stable state. This finding provides a more intricate understanding of nonlocal effects, revealing that they can be complex and varied, and that single-particle nonlocality alone is capable of exhibiting a rich and dynamic behavior. This research also discovers a previously unknown connection between single-particle nonlocality and stability. The nonlocal effects that arise from a single particle can be thought of as a form of entanglement that exists across space, and that binds the particle to its environment. This perspective is similar to the idea proposed by Ghirardi, Rimini, and Weber, which is a stochastic and non-reversible formulation of the Schrödinger equation. The relationship between single-particle nonlocality and stability suggests that the collapse of space-time must be spontaneous, as prompted by the presence of single-particle nonlocality. The fundamental reason for this hypothesis remains unknown, but it provides a potential answer to the question of why the collapse of space-time should be spontaneous. The study of single-particle nonlocality in this context highlights the connection between the stochastic Schrödinger equation and the issue of time, which underlies the dynamics of the universe. The integration of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) technologies and automotive education systems holds great promise in creating a safe and efficient transportation environment. IoV education systems are being developed to train sophisticated machine learning models that can ensure vehicle autonomy. However, the significant amount of data required for these models necessitates the development of secure and efficient learning mechanisms. In response to these challenges, a novel concept known as Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning (BELF) has emerged as a promising solution. A framework based on BELF has been proposed to provide a secure and collaborative platform for IoV education systems through federated learning. This paper surveys the development of BELF-based IoV education systems, presenting an examination of the existing research and potential directions for future development. This work also contributes a conceptual design for a BELF-based IoV education framework, along with a discussion of various research approaches and potential challenges. This survey is intended to guide further innovation and provide a foundation for ongoing research in this domain. This paper is targeted towards a broad academic audience interested in IoV education systems, BELF technology, and related applications. This survey is further categorized into the following subtopics: (1) IoV education systems, (2) BELF technology, and (3) research papers integrating BELF and IoV education systems. This work presents a comprehensive literature review of 120 cited papers, covering the period from 2010 to 2023. This survey is primarily published in the journal IEEE Communications Standards Advanced Reports and Updates. This paper is an extension of a previous standard advancement notification titled "Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning Framework for IoV Education Systems." This paper is also related to two other published papers titled "BelFiery: A Secure and Efficient Federated Learning System for IoV" and "FEDERATED-NS: A BelFiery-Based Federated Learning Platform for Dynamic Network Scheduling in IoV." In FDD systems, codebooks and feedback encoding play a significant role in minimizing channel state variation costs. Codebooks are designed to efficiently map reduced-dimensional features to full-dimensional channels, ultimately improving system performance. Codebooks can be viewed as implementations of Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), which effectively capture channel distribution patterns. By redefining codebook construction as a GMM learning problem, we develop an efficient method to create codebooks, leveraging the availability of accurate GMM-based estimation tools. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the development of adaptive codebooks, enabling real-time adjustment to changing channel conditions. In addition to codebook construction, we also explore GMM-based encoding techniques to minimize feedback data costs, including a novel general-purpose scheme and a more specialized option for correlated channels. Our research is validated through extensive numerical testing, revealing performance benefits across various scenario complexities. Our codebook and feedback encoding methods are publicly available on GitHub. The findings presented in this work have been published in the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications and IEEE Communications Letters. The contributions have also been presented at the IEEE International Conference on Communications, the IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference, and the IEEE Global Communications Conference. The codebase developed from this research has been licensed to the company Alphabetha Technologies for further commercialization. The current research focus has been on expanding the codebook development framework to support machine learning-based prediction methods, as well as investigating more efficient encoding schemes to reduce feedback data costs. The objectives of these ongoing research efforts are to enhance performance in scenarios with significant channel state variation and to provide viable solutions for real-world applications. To understand the intricate behavior of nonequilibrium surface steps in fcc crystals, a reliable theoretical framework is lacking, especially when considering two-dimensional bulk conditions. However, a recent statistical model has successfully explained various phenomena, ranging from the stabilization of steps to their destructive pattern formation, relying solely on the interplay between thermal fluctuations, lattice asymmetry, and particle flow. In this study, we apply this nonequilibrium statistical model to the 3D Hofstadter model, a well-studied model of statistical mechanics on a lattice with time-reversal symmetry, and find that it accurately describes the average spacing between dislocations that form along the surface. Additionally, we observe that the topological character of the Hofstadter model leads to quantized space-filling patterns and massive disorder in the far nonequilibrium region. Furthermore, we find that the distribution of average dislocation spacings exhibits a sudden and significant shift as the flux through the lattice changes, albeit for specific, integrally quantized values. The integration quantization arises from the interplay between the particle's periodic motion and the asymmetric lattice, resulting in a series of sharp steps in the distribution of spacings that mirror the underlying physics of the Hofstadter model. The model's applicability is demonstrated across a range of conditions, including both weak and intense particle-flow regimes, and the results are experimentally relevant, given that the 3D Hofstadter model can be replicated using a combination of optical lattices and magnetic flux, making it possible to visually observe the predicted patterns of spacings and dislocation formation with high resolution. The model can further be applied to analyze surface flows in other systems, such as solid-state materials with magnetic impurities, optical lattices with magnetic disorder, and coupled oscillators in chemistry and biology. For a self-gravitating object under stress, the rate of change of the mass is determined by the rate of change of the surface area, and this relationship can be expressed through the Einstein field equations. In 1920, Bondi first proposed this connection, which for a spherical object in asymptotic flatness leads to the rate of change of mass being proportional to the square of the rate of change of the surface area. Using observations of quasars and their associated gravitational waves, researchers have been able to place constraints on the rate of change of mass. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding and generating effective actions.
One notable reason these games have gained significant attention is due to their connection to real-world conversations.
However, a major limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 moves per second, largely because of the simple Python-based framework used to power them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely-used text-based game challenges, achieving an astonishing increase in simulation speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On machines featuring multiple GPUs, we observed speeds of over one million moves per second, enabling the creation of comprehensive evaluations involving millions of moves in a fraction of the time required previously. Our findings also highlight best practices for rapidly optimizing complex programs like text-based games, with strategies applicable to a broad range of computational tasks. Ultimately, our advanced framework and accompanying results demonstrate significant progress towards developing incredibly rigorous and time-consuming evaluation methods for virtual agent abilities in tasks centered on natural language. Our code is available at https://github.com/tristandekker/textworldexpress.

Essentially, given two copies of the same conformal field theory, one coupled to a semi-simple gauge group and the other standalone, can we determine the conformal field theory coupled to the gauge group as a subsector? In an attempt to address this, we examine charged elements within a conformally invariant theory, with the aim of establishing a connection to the parent theory from which the conformally invariant theory is derived. The feeble gravity conjecture, a proposed extension of the tHooft polymaton duality, emerges as a framework that provides convictions on this front, including the conviction that charged elements within a conformally invariant theory are convex. Through the use of a specific conformally invariant theory with charged elements, we demonstrate that convexity is not a universally inherent property, thus disproving the feeble gravity conjecture in its current form. Nonetheless, the rejection of the feeble gravity conjecture in its current iteration does not preclude the possibility of its extension to a more comprehensive form that could potentially incorporate convexity as a fundamental property of conformally invariant theories. In such a case, the theory with charged elements presented in this study could be seen as an illustration of the concept of feeble gravity near the specific regime being examined. This paper investigates solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in the presence of a convex barrier, specifically in the region outside the barrier where the solution has a positive energy. We find that solutions with a specific initial condition, those in the "explosion" category, will expand to infinity in both time and space. Additionally, we determine that in the case of a bounded barrier, these solutions eventually reach an infinite state in a finite amount of time. Furthermore, we establish that solutions with a different initial condition are not generated by the solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier, even when the initial condition has a negative energy. This result holds true for the scenario with a bounded barrier and holds asymptotically true for the scenario with an unbounded barrier. We also demonstrate that the behavior of solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a star-shaped barrier is comparable to the behavior of solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier. We establish this comparison by showing that there are solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier for any given star-shaped barrier, specifically those solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of the convex barrier formed by the curve defined by the initial data. We demonstrate this statement to be true for the scenario with a bounded barrier and hold asymptotically true for the scenario with an unbounded barrier. We also investigate the relationship between solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier and solutions with a negative energy in the outside region of the same barrier, finding that solutions with a negative energy are not generated by solutions with a positive energy, even in the asymptotic limit for the scenario with an unbounded barrier. We further analyze the problem by considering solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier as being composed of a sum of solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of the barrier at a given time, providing an expression for the $H^1$ norm of these solutions. We also derive an inequality that relates the $H^1$ norm of solutions with a positive energy in the outside region of a convex barrier at a given time to the $H^1$ norm of the initial condition, specifically that the $H^1$ norm of the solutions at a later time is greater than the $H^1$ norm of the initial condition multiplied by the square root of the difference between the energy of the solutions at the later time and the energy of the solutions at the initial time.

This research introduces a novel numerical method to model single-phase Darcy flow within porous media containing fractures. Fractures in this model are characterized as high-permeability channels with arbitrary orientation, causing them to interface with surrounding porous media of varying levels of permeability. Due to the significant differences in fracture and media permeability, flow behavior near fractures is determined using the Navier-Stokes equations, whereas overall flow patterns are captured using the Lagrangian method. A Lagrangian approach is chosen to model flow outside fractures as it allows for the tracking of fluid particles and thus better captures streamlines and boundary obstacles. The integration of these two methods is achieved through a combination of finite element solutions for flow within fractures and Lagrangian simulations for flow outside fractures. The position of fractures is represented by meshed surfaces within the Lagrangian simulation, enabling the detection of surface interactions between fractures and surrounding media and the validation of boundary conditions. The proposed technique includes three key parts: (1) the representation of fractures within the Lagrangian simulation, (2) the determination of flow outside fractures, and (3) the integration of flow outside and within fractures. The development of this method also includes the derivation of hybrid-combined equations for flow outside fractures as well as the derivation of a numerical scheme for time-dependent flow. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through the simulation of flow around moving boundaries and the comparison of this method with other established approaches through the simulation of flow in porous media containing fractures. The proposed technique offers a more efficient and accurate numerical method for modeling flow in porous media containing fractures by reducing the number of finite element nodes required for simulation. The development of this method is further taken a step further with the creation of a computational code capable of modeling two-dimensional flow in porous media containing moving boundaries. The possibilities for enhancing this method include the integration of mass transport simulations within the proposed framework. The proposed technique has also been tested on a real-world scenario of flow in a fractured rock mass with various rock massfulness factors. The outcomes of these simulations have been compared with outcomes obtained using other numerical methods such as Finite Element and Finite Difference methods. In written communication between humans and AI, certain discourse markers such as "however" and "nevertheless" convey similar meanings, yet their implications vary. For example, "however" usually signals a contradiction, whereas "nevertheless" implies a smoother transition between ideas. Despite this distinction, existing automatic tools to analyze discourse markers focus primarily on their basic definitions, without considering the context in which they are used, the effect they have on the structure of a text, or the specific purposes of communication they serve. As a result, researchers and developers who work with discourse markers may gain limited insight from these tools. To address this shortcoming, we present a method for examining discourse markers based on their functional characteristics, and we have implemented this approach in a tool called DiscSense. This tool allows users to explore discourse markers across various contexts, including their prevalence on the web, their use in specific domains, the context in which they appear, and the changes they cause to the underlying meaning of a piece of text. Furthermore, DiscSense features a graphical interface that illustrates the relationship between discourse markers and the purpose of communication they serve, and it provides interactive tools for navigating these relationships in different contexts. We have tested this tool on a subset of articles from a well-known academic journal and a large collection of web pages, and our results show that DiscSense reveals meaningful information about the way discourse markers are used in real-world communication. Our tool is available online, and we invite users to explore its features and provide feedback on its performance. Our research on DiscSense also contributes a new dataset of annotated discourse markers, which is unique in that it takes into account the context in which they are used, and it differs from existing datasets that focus primarily on their basic definitions. This new dataset is currently limited to web pages, but we plan to expand it to include other types of text. Our tool and dataset are designed to help researchers who work with discourse markers, and they are available online for download. Our tool has the potential to be integrated into various applications that involve written communication between humans and AI, and it can be used to provide feedback to users on the way discourse markers are used in their writing. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the satisfiability issue with a particular type of regular expression known as Extended Regular Expressions (ERE). Unlike traditional regular expressions, EREs incorporate both logical disjunction and conjunction in their expressions. Our research introduces a new decision-making approach that utilizes resolution principles to synthesize ERE inequalities. We also established that our algorithm's efficiency is comparable to the complexity of the regular language's membership problem. Furthermore, we demonstrated that both our approach and a comparable method from the literature share the same temporal complexity (O(n^2)). Additionally, we explored the potential extension of our method to other types of regular expressions and examined a specific case study involving string matching against databases of varying sizes. The underlying principle of our method, however, is inherently compatible with the environment of the satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solving framework, allowing for the integration of external learning capabilities. The developed algorithm is now available as an open-source tool for solving ERE inequalities within the Z3 SMT solver. The research also includes a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance, along with a concrete case study of string matching against a database of one million strings. The developed tool has successfully solved this instance in approximately one second. The developed algorithm has a single scalar variable, and its execution serves as an instance of the bigger class of iteration methods for deciding the satisfiability of first-order formulas over monoidal structures. The research provides an open-ended question regarding the extension of the algorithm to higher-dimensional variables. The developed tool is unique in its capacity to handle conjunction within regular expressions among the existing solvers, and it outperforms them significantly when conjunction is present, based on an evaluation conducted using a broad set of randomly generated inequalities. The research also includes an appendix containing a formal definition of the EREs along with an explanation of the resolution rule from a grammatical perspective. Recently, visual-inertial navigation techniques have been highly successful in determining an observer's position and orientation without the need for external references. These systems achieve this without the significant distortion caused by self-taught optimization issues and limited sensor data, by utilizing recurrent models that combine temporal information. In this research, we deviate from this trend and develop an external memory attention-based model, known as EMA-VIO, to tackle self-biasing and integrate the available sensory data. Our proposed method incorporates an attention-based model that focuses on relevant memory locations, combined with a state transition and measurement update process, to estimate the current state. Our results show that EMA-VIO outperforms state-of-the-art visual-inertial navigation models and compares favorably to systems that rely on external GPS signals, based on both simulation and real-world data. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Jeffrey-He/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, yet the properties of a specific class of materials, called Weyl semimetals, stem solely from the high-order components of a vector, specifically the imaginary part of a complex scalar.  This unique characteristic allows an unusual transformation that raises the semimetal's low-order scalar component to a vector, resulting in a novel state of matter called "square-root elevated-order Weyl semimetal," and gives rise to an unusual four-fermion interaction in its spectrum.  This new state of matter can be realized in a simple two-dimensional lattice constructed from square loops and possesses a topological phase indicator that distinguishes it from other topological materials.  Our findings indicate that this novel state of matter can be stable in a three-dimensional space and allow for the direct observation of its unique properties using a range of experiments including spectroscopy, transport, and surface topology.  We also show that this state of matter can be modified to resemble other exotic states of matter, such as square-loop Weyl semimetals, Dirac fermions, and square-shaped topological insulators.  Our simulations demonstrate that this state of matter is accessible and stable using a range of materials, including strontium, titanium, and osmium, and predict the possible detection of its unique properties using high-energy particle beams, for example the discovery of monopole currents and the resulting chiral anomaly, as well as the unique four-fermion emission associated with it.  Our research opens up a new and versatile platform for exploring the unique properties of four-fermion interactions, the stability of ferromagnetic order, the generation of topological edge states, and the interaction between defect-induced monopoles and the surrounding material.

Leveraging deep learning is crucial for automating information extraction from visually complex documents, but generating a large-scale labeled dataset for this purpose is a significant obstacle due to its high cost.  Our proposed approach, called Semi-Supervised Document Learning (SSDL), tackles this challenge by minimizing the number of labels required.  SSDL incorporates a combined model that combines supervised training with strategic selection of partially labeled documents, offering a cost-effective route to high-performance models.  Our framework can be applied across various applications, including but not limited to, information extraction from visually complex documents.  We have tested SSDL on real-world datasets involving financial documents and credit contract extracts, achieving superior results compared to existing methods.  Our findings demonstrate that with as little as 100 partially labeled documents, SSDL can achieve the same level of accuracy as models trained on 5000 fully labeled documents.  Our code is available at https://github.com/PranavGopi.

We define a differentiable structure on locally arching spaces and demonstrate that it meets the requirements of a natural geometric object. Furthermore, we establish that integration over these spaces holds according to the standard formula, providing a basis for the application of techniques from differential geometry and the theory of differential forms to locally arching spaces. Additionally, our approach allows us to generalize the Stokes theorem for these spaces. Moreover, we show that our definition of a differentiable structure is consistent with that of a differentiable manifold when the latter is defined using the notion of local coordinates. Moreover, we demonstrate that the concept of differentiable structure on locally arching spaces is independent of the specific formulation, and we provide two alternative descriptions of it. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between locally arching spaces and differential forms in a way that generalizes the relationship between these concepts in the context of manifold theory.

This work examines the impact of a space's curvature on stochastic field models, using a mathematical framework that incorporates the field's natural variability. We show that the Gaussian stochastic field's expected behavior is directly related to the underlying geometry, and that the standard approach to defining intrinsic averaging techniques can be recovered when the stochastic field is fully analyzed and its natural variability is accounted for. Furthermore, we determine that the mean of a Gaussian stochastic field is equivalent to the geometric mean of the underlying space, and that this relationship can be extended to the stochastic field's covariance when the space's curvature is characterized by a specific mathematical property called symmetry. This property is demonstrated through synthetic data generated in both flat and curved spaces, and the results are applied to the analysis of a realistic dataset generated in a fractal landscape. The approach presented in this work provides a practical method for constructing Gaussian stochastic field models that accurately reflect a space's underlying geometry and natural variability. High-performance computing on GPUs requires efficient memory management, and current approaches often limit concurrency to achieve this efficiency. This performance trade-off is particularly detrimental for object-based programming, which naturally fosters concurrent operations but is often inhibited on GPUs. To address this challenge, we present DynaSOAr, a state-of-the-art, concurrent memory allocator tailored specifically for object-based programming on GPUs. DynaSOAr employs a hybrid allocation strategy, combining a large, coarse-grained free memory pool with smaller, fine-grained chunks available for rapid allocation and deallocation. This design enables efficient and concurrent allocation and deallocation across large memory spaces on GPUs. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's unique pool structure allows for direct insertion of new memory chunks, bypassing lock acquisition, which significantly accelerates insertion efficiency and reduces concurrency restrictions. In addition to its concurrent memory allocation features, DynaSOAr includes advanced memory packing and formatting techniques that minimize memory waste and align data with GPU requirements, thereby optimizing memory usage and performance. We present a simple, object-based programming model called SOAR, which leverages DynaSOAr's capabilities and provides relevant benchmark results showing that DynaSOAr-based implementations outperform conventional approaches on GPUs in various categories, including scientific computing, machine learning, and object-based simulations. We also make DynaSOAr and related materials available online for public use.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model, applicable to all impurity states, incorporates the effects of spin-orbit interaction, magnetic anisotropy, and scattering of electrons off the superconducting surface. It provides an in-depth understanding of the spectral features associated with the Kondo effect, including the emergence of zero-bias peaks and the shift of the Peierls phase, which are influenced by the orientation of the spin quadrupole and the magnetic field. Furthermore, this model has been utilized to analyze the spectra of individual manganese atoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface, offering a detailed explanation of previous observations and predicting additional phenomena, such as the splitting of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state in dimers and the formation of a pair-bound state in the limit where the spin remains frozen. It also predicts the occurrence of a pair-breaking state at a particular orientation of the spin quadrupole component, characterized by the presence of a finite amplitude of the $d_{z^2}$ state and a corresponding zero-bias peak in the density of states. This model is particularly relevant to recent experiments involving manganese impurities on the Nb(110) surface and offers a comprehensive understanding of their spectral characteristics. Additionally, it facilitates prediction of new phenomena that can be verified through subsequent experiments. Moreover, this theoretical framework is applicable to other systems, such as manganese impurities on the Ni(111) surface, and can be extended to include interactions between distant impurities by incorporating a semiclassical approach to their electronic properties. It is also notable that this model can be simplified to better match experimental capabilities, such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, by using a specific basis set that yields a compact and intuitive description of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. It is further found that the critical thickness of the superconducting layer is directly influenced by the strength of the spin-orbit interaction and the magnetic anisotropy of the impurity, which can take on various values depending on the orientation, Demel-Kohn, or Mott localization of the $d$ electrons. It is also demonstrated that the model can be applied to investigate the effects of the spin-orbit interaction and magnetic anisotropy on the critical thickness of the superconducting layer, offering a theoretical understanding of the related phenomena and providing a predictive framework for future experiments. Our study of titanium dioxide rutile using density functional theory explores the impact of carbon and nitrogen impurities on this material's band structure and magnetic properties. By examining the effects of different impurity arrangements and concentrations, we gained insight into how the arrangement of $p$-electrons and magnetic fields are affected by the presence of these impurities. Our findings indicate that both carbon and nitrogen can induce magnetic properties in titanium dioxide rutile, although the degree to which this happens varies depending on the concentration of the impurities. Specifically, we found that a concentration of 6.25% can result in half-filled bands and might be particularly useful for implementing the Mott-Hubbard model. Our research also analyzed the binding energies of these impurities, which range from 5.13 eV for oxygen-like states in carbon, to 7.46 eV for nitrogen, and 6.57 eV for oxygen-like states in titanium, as well as the effects of different impurity arrangements on the material's band structure and magnetic properties. We also identified possible sites for nitrogen and carbon impurities based on experimental information, which could help with interpreting spectra of the material. Finally, our study predicted that both carbon and nitrogen can form dimer structures under certain conditions, which could help with understanding their effects on the material's band structure and magnetic properties, and also provided expressions for the energies of these dimers in terms of the lattice constant and concentration of the impurities. This earlier conjecture from 1991 suggested that in any two-colored division of an infinitely large graph, there exists a monochromatic subgraph consisting of a specified pattern. The 1993 proof by Erdos, Spinka, and Galvin demonstrated the validity of this conjecture, which is equivalent to a 1978 conjecture of Erdos and Galvin. The non-relativistic, massless QED model known as scalar Quantum Electrodynamics (sQED) exhibits a highly interesting phase structure. It possesses a concave term in its free energy and a significant critical behavior, thereby making it an outstanding subject of study. However, implementing this model becomes computationally complex when using quantum simulators, especially when moving beyond a few qubits. A recent achievement has made it possible to employ multiple qutrits in quantum simulations of the 1+1D sQED model, following a proper mapping of the bosonic field in terms of Fock states rather than the traditional field mapping. This new approach allows for sound excitations that can be observed, in contrast to the static properties seen in previous simulations. A key finding of this research reveals that the sound excitations exhibit a critical point when analyzed, which can be detected through the average sound speed. This result demonstrates that sound excitations serve as an excellent indicator of the quantum phase transition, offering a more versatile probe of the underlying physics. Furthermore, sound excitations provide a promising outcome for experimental verification, given the readily accessible sound speed in comparison to the static energy density or the Casimir effect. This development paves the way for exploring the physics of sQED using qutrits in quantum simulations and offers a valuable lesson on the importance of sound excitations as an experimental marker in this subject. Finally, this finding is anticipated to extend beyond sQED to other field-theory models exhibiting phase transitions and sound excitations. The new approach using Fock states also facilitates the inclusion of particle losses, thereby providing a more realistic simulation of the model. The achievement of employing sound excitations as an indicator of the quantum phase transition in sQED was made possible using a specific simulation platform, yet it is anticipated that this result will be applicable to other quantum simulation devices involving qutrits. The development of this new approach is further seen as a means of exploring the interplay between collective behavior and losses in qutrit systems. The simulation of sound excitations in sQED can be implemented using a range of simulation languages, including Tensor Network, Tensor Network Algorithms, and Quantum Simulation Platforms, among others. The inclusion of losses in the simulation involves implementing an additional term in the Hamiltonian, for example by utilizing Tensor Network Algorithms. The investigation of sound excitations in sQED additionally opens up the possibility of examining other models involving field-theory, as well as models involving sound excitations in condensed matter systems.

Research indicates that ultra-intense laser interactions with thin materials may create significant polarization in positron beams. To explore the potential of a different setup, we examined positron polarization produced when ultra-intense lasers illuminate thick targets. Utilizing the "Polarstrating Shell" model, especially developed for this study, we found that the degree of polarization can reach up to 90% for a specific range of positron energies. Furthermore, polarization persists even in deeper layers of the target, allowing for the extraction of highly polarized positrons from longer targets as well. By comparing our findings with existing research on thin targets, we observed that the polarization degree remains largely unaffected by changes in energy, despite the expected increase according to theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, our study reveals that the polarization degree will increase in thinner layers of a longer target, given the same conditions. Our work began as a modification of the "Polarstrating Shell" model to also take into account the effects of photon splitting, but unfortunately, this complication cannot be modeled and may limit the accuracy of our results. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that thick targets are preferable for producing highly polarized positron beams in the context of laser-plasma based positron polarization. This work was a part of the author's PhD research completed under the supervision of Dr. Gary Barton-Shonewille and Dr. Ronan Kilgallon at the University of Leeds. The research was supported by the STFC and the Royal Society. The computational simulations were carried out on the University of Leeds's HPC facility, BRIDGE, and the data analysis was performed using Python, Mathematica, and the "Polarstrating Shell" model. The model has been made available online for public use. The research has been published in the journal Physics of Plasmas, with the paper's title "Thick Polarized Positrons from Laser-Illuminated Foil Targets in the QED Regime". We establish that any function computable in a circuit of a limited type, consisting of $n$ variables, can be expressed as a polynomial of degree one higher than the circuit's top layer, with coefficients determined by the circuit's structural parameters. Additionally, we show that functions computable in a limited group $(G, \cdot,^{-1})$ with a specific property associated to its group elements can be represented by a polynomial of a specific degree, and we determine this degree to be equivalent to the smallest integer exceeding the average degree of the polynomial associated with each group element. Our results extend and improve existing formulas for functions associated with limited groups, and our approach introduces a new method for translating formula estimates to polynomial representations. Our research also implies that any function computable in a limited group can be approximately represented as a polynomial of a specific degree, and we establish a connection between this representation and the availability of efficient learning algorithms for these functions. Our main contribution is the development of a theoretical framework for evaluating the efficiency of circuit-based learning algorithms, and we believe this framework has value beyond just limited groups. Our research also addresses some previous open problems, and our approach provides a new perspective on the relationship between circuit-based learning and efficient polynomial approximations. Our results further validate a recent conjecture regarding the efficiency of a particular circuit-based learning algorithm and provide a higher bound on the efficacy of this algorithm. Our approach is composed of a pre-processing phase where we develop a compact formula estimating the output of the circuit for each possible input, and a main synthesis phase where we create a new circuit based on this compact formula. Our approach is flexible and can be applied to different types of limited groups, and we provide two examples of this versatility. This research develops a miniaturized temperature detector using 90nm transistors, enabling precise temperature measurements while considering process variations and voltage fluctuations. The design employs a $PMOS$ threshold voltage to minimize precision loss and counteracts the effect of $V_{th}$ distribution through a source series connection. A comprehensive analysis takes into account both statistical and systematic variations, yielding a temperature resolution of 0.24°C with a voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V and a power consumption of 2.5nW. Furthermore, the design exhibits a small area of 2% of a standard $NMOS$ ring oscillator and a high speed of a 1.5µs conversion time. The proposed temperature detector can be applied in various fields including cryptographic systems, microprocessors, and memory chips, and its efficiency has been validated through silicon measurements of a 4µm$^2$ device operating across a wide temperature range. The measurement results confirm the design's effectiveness and demonstrate a precise temperature measurement capability with a precision of 0.24°C, a maximum error of 1.4°C, and a low power consumption of 2.5nW. This research paper focuses on two main concepts from geometry: Lie groupoids and stacks. Lie groupoids represent a non-abative generalization of Lie groups, while stacks can be seen as non-abative versions of moduli spaces. Both of these concepts have extensive uses in physics and mathematics, particularly in solving problems related to boundary value scenarios, among other applications. Our study aims to expand the theory of geometric configurations from these domains by incorporating vector fields, forms, and bundles within the framework of groupoids and stacks. We demonstrate how existing results about Lie groups can be applied to groupoids by utilizing descent techniques. Additionally, we establish a connection between the geometric configurations on a stack and the geometric configurations on certain associated Lie groups through the use of base change functors. This connection serves as a fundamental ingredient in developing the notion of smooth morphisms between stacks. Our study also delves into the study of vector bundles, forms, and vector fields on Lie groupoids and stacks, along with the associated differential operators such as the exterior differential, the Lie derivative, and the Hodge star operator. We show that these fundamental operators behave consistently on the geometric configurations on a stack and its associated Lie groups, enabling us to extend the concept of smooth bundles, forms, and vectors to the realm of stacks. We conclude our study by examining the relationship between the geometric configurations on a stack and the associated groupoids, along with exploring the concept of algebraic structures on stacks. Our research also yields several notable results, including but not limited to: the development of vector bundles, forms, and vector fields on Lie groupoids and stacks; the extension of the exterior differential, the Lie derivative, and the Hodge star operator to the realm of stacks; and the discovery that the behavior of bundles, forms, and vector fields on a stack is directly linked to the behavior of their associated groupoids. We further investigate the algebraic structures on stacks by considering examples such as stacks associated with Lie algebras, Lie superalgebras, and Jordan algebras. The second section delves into the theoretical foundations of geometric configurations on Lie groupoids, while the third section explores the same concept on stacks. The detection of cancerous cells is crucial, and doctors rely on histopathology images to diagnose skin carcinoma. However, identifying these images can be difficult and time-consuming due to the intricate details and similar appearances between cancerous and benign cells. In addition to challenges doctors face, they also tend to misclassify typical abnormal patterns as normal tissue, which can delay critical treatment decisions. To address these issues, a deep learning framework is proposed that not only detects cancerous cells but also identifies unusual patterns that are often misinterpreted as normal tissue. The proposed method involves two consecutive steps: first, a network called ResNeXt is used to classify images as cancerous or benign, and then a second network based on attention mechanisms and ReLU activates is used to identify unusual patterns that may be cancerous. The effectiveness of the proposed method and the need for only two images are demonstrated through experiments conducted on three datasets. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy and detects unusual patterns that are consistent with clinical standards. The proposed method has the potential to be a valuable tool for both medical professionals and students by learning the features of cancerous and benign cells and helping them differentiate between normal and abnormal patterns. The proposed method can also be applied to other biological disciplines beyond dermatology. The behavior of a growing interface in a pattern of periodic scratches on a rotating plate, held by a frame that is slowly moved apart, is examined in a Hele-Shaw cell filled with a viscous liquid containing small amounts of gas. Despite the dynamic conditions, the interface fingers can maintain a steady width, despite increasing distance and speed of the frame. The development of the interface is analyzed in a variety of configurations, demonstrating how the width of the fingers is influenced by the rate of frame movement and the presence of bubbles. The process is also looked at with a variety of frame shapes and patterns of scratches. The movement of the frame and the resulting finger development can be slowed down by increasing the rotation speed of the plate. The process has been simulated in a numerical model, confirming the observed patterns of finger development. The model shows that the width of the fingers is determined by the balance between the force driving the interface apart and the friction holding it in place, taking into account the curved shape of the plate and the presence of bubbles. The model also shows that the plate can be thought of as a set of connected points, pressing the interface apart at the points where the scratches meet. The shape of the fingers is influenced by the shape of the plate, showing how the plate's shape affects the width of the fingers in a variety of configurations. The process is distinct from other experiments with spinning plates and scratches, developing a long, curved interface that can return to a circular shape if the plate is slowed down. The process is related to other growing interface experiments, such as the spinning drop and the spinning disk, but differs from them by maintaining a steady width in a pattern of scratches. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. However, precision is often compromised due to limited access to patients' full side views resulting from the curved surface of scanners. This research introduces the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method to enhance the accuracy of lateral shift estimations in elastography. By generating synthetic aperture data based on the assumption of a flat surface, and combining it with actual scanner data, the method achieves unbiased lateral shift estimations and APAs (average absolute errors) of 2.8 mm in fatty and 4.0 mm in muscular tissues. Furthermore, with the integration of regularised Fourier transform, the method effectively removes speckle noise from elastography images. The proposed approach is suitable for various scanner configurations and can be efficiently implemented using an Intel Core i7 computer within a 10 ms time frame. The results of VOSA are compared to the state-of-the-art methods CWS and CSD, demonstrating the advantages of this novel technique. The development of the VOSA algorithm, along with simulation and experimental validation, is presented in this paper. This paper introduces a novel framework for stochastic games that incorporates both pursuit-and-evade and pursuit-withdrawal elements, bridging the gap between these two extreme cases. We establish a hierarchical division of the game state space, employing relative entropy and a partition function to compute important probabilities. This hierarchy enables the construction of efficient algorithms to determine optimal value functions and determine the game's outcome, all while maintaining a linear computational complexity in the size of the state space. Furthermore, we establish a straightforward yet precise bound on the expected discounted reward for the pursuer, leveraging the hierarchy's structure and a control theory approach. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework to various scenarios, including hierarchical division, by providing concrete examples and presenting possible modifications to the basic framework. These adaptations include the use of multiple pursuers, a changing game landscape, and the inclusion of punishment for capture. These extensions illustrate the framework's versatility and the utility of hierarchical divisions in a broader context. The paper's conclusions are accompanied by a discussion of potential future research directions. This research focuses on developing an efficient method for detecting vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon collisions. Due to the vast amount of data involved, a fast vector boson estimation approach is crucial for historical muon data. To achieve this, we propose two metrics: the average transverse momentum of hadrons associated with a muon pair, and the acoplanarity of these pairs. We found that estimating the mass of vector bosons using these two metrics provides accurate results, especially for higher energy collisions. Specifically, using the collinearity of a muon pair and the average transverse momentum of its associated hadrons allows us to distinguish between W and Z bosons with about 90% accuracy, which increases to 95% when considering the charge of the muons. We further analyzed the characteristics of hadron associated complexes, describing how their properties vary with energy and suggesting that, in many cases, they can be distinguished based on these characteristics alone. To validate our results, we compared our method to the underlying physics using Monte Carlo simulations, which supported our findings. We also explored ways to improve our method by incorporating charge information and developing a more precise estimator for the transverse mass of vector bosons. We introduce a novel model where four mobile agents, inspired by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser, navigate through the plane to gather at a specifically designated meeting point. Each agent's path is defined by a differential equation based on the directions they take, with the goal of achieving a particular angle between their trajectories. We investigate several key aspects of this system in the context of the plane, including its structure, the set of possible states it can occupy, and the gathering scenario with four agents. Our analysis reveals that the system's state space consists of two distinct components: a planar disk and a semi-torus. In the case of the plane and the semi-torus, we determine the conditions under which the system can gather seamlessly. However, on the annulus, we find that the system's behavior is more complex and depends on the specific parameters, while on the circle, the system cannot gather for most of the time. Our study also discusses the relationship between the system's state and the angles formed by the agents' paths, as well as the impact of adding a boundary to the system. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to demonstrate the effects of different parameters on the system's performance. Lastly, we offer an interpretation of this model as a metaphor for the interconnection of different mathematical formalisms. The underlying system can be extended to mimic the behavior of mobile robots in the presence of obstacles, as well as in the presence of errors or delays. The model has significant implications for the theory of partial differential equations, specifically in the context of the Birkhoff normal form, and may find applications in the study of nonlinear Schrödinger equations, as well as in the analysis of the complexity of finite state automata. The associated source code is available at https://github.com/mbartuccelli/GTRC. The corresponding numerical toolbox can be used to solve a broad range of PDEs, including those associated with the circular Foucault theorem, the Geyer-Rossler metric, and the Navier-Stokes equations, among others. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolution layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach and pitched-based content and pitch-related convolution filters, yet its computationally expensive training process and generation time remain significant challenges. To overcome these limitations and expand WN's pitch control to quasi-periodic signals, we introduce a generative framework consisting of multiple stacked WN components with varying period lengths, seamlessly blended through dilated convolution neural networks to ensure smooth periodicity, thus enhancing the model's flexibility and ability to generate quasi-periodic data. Experimental evaluations on both speech and musical genres demonstrate the versatility of QPNet, offering a scalable and efficient solution for a range of generative tasks, from raw waveform synthesis to music compression. Compared to current state-of-the-art models, QPNet achieves significant performance gains while generating high-fidelity audio at a lower computational cost, also enabling real-time audio synthesis. The proposed model's versatility is further illustrated by modifying QPNet to create a speech encoder, which demonstrates an improvement in intelligence scores and is suitable for various speech processing tasks. The code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Shoukai-Liu/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

To facilitate efficient determination of sound sources, a new algorithm is introduced, leveraging a 3D grid to identify the sound's point of origin through simple calculations used by the eardrum-conveyed signals. The results show that the method accurately determines the sound's point of origin, even with distant sounds and multiple sound sources present at the same time. The method's efficiency is also shown to increase with the distance of the sound sources from the subject. The proposed technology has significant potential benefits for various applications, including audio communication for deaf individuals, military operations, concerts, and public gatherings, among others. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex and non-euclidean data, and there's a growing interest in developing GNNs that can operate on graphs with a positive definite manifold. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for defining GNNs on positive definite manifolds, and demonstrate the versatility of this framework by incorporating multiple positive definite manifolds within a single graph. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on datasets that incorporate linear subspaces, non-linear subspaces, and circular manifolds, and our method is found to surpass existing techniques. We also explore the properties of our model and discover that it is influenced by a variety of factors, including the network's depth, width, and initialization, as well as the hyperparameters of the optimizer. Our research also enables us to successfully train a GNN on a complex dataset with a multi-linear manifold. We hope that this work will serve as a foundation for future research on GNNs, especially those dealing with heterogeneous data and multi-manifold graphs. Our code is available at https://github.com/LC-1024/LGNNSimple.

Reconstructing acoustic structures and their attached components from recorded sound waves is a complex problem with many possible solutions. However, for many applications, it's not enough to simply recover the underlying geometry, but rather to determine the precise characteristics of the acoustic structure and the components attached to it, including the positions, types, and properties of objects within the scene. This challenge becomes even more complex in scenarios involving multiple non-rigid structures, multiple attached objects, and varying sound frequencies, where the recovery of surface geometry, material properties, and the positions and types of attached objects must be accomplished simultaneously. This research presents a novel approach to addressing this highly demanding task of acoustic structure and component recovery, and presents the results of this approach's effectiveness through numerical experiments. This method has been tested on synthetic data and has shown superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art method of acoustic inverse problem solving. In this paper, we introduce an novel exponential delay model inspired by Tsallis statistics, which is a contraction compared to the standard exponential delay model. This new model serves as an extension to the standard model, and we derive its expectations and second moments. Furthermore, we investigate its implications for the memory characteristics of an autoregressive process, and demonstrate that it leads to a process with long-term memory properties. Additionally, we analyze the Tsallis delay model's behavior as a special case, and show that it reduces to an autoregressive process with long memory properties when the delay parameter satisfies a particular condition. This process can be compared to the standard exponential delay model, and we investigate the differences it makes when applied to financial data. Lastly, we discuss the Tsallis delay model's connections to other models, and examine its statistical properties to determine if it provides a better fit to financial time series data compared to the standard exponential delay model. This model's performance is compared to the standard exponential delay model and ARFIMA models, and we investigate its financial applications by using it to estimate the long-memory properties of financial indices. Lastly, we conclude our study by discussing the Tsallis delay model's and its potential ramifications. This work is part of the doctoral research of M.M. at Yildiz Technical University. This representation utilizes classical Fourier transforms and provides an intuitive understanding of how quantum correlations are established and maintained through interactions with environmental systems. This research proposes a novel concept, termed relative quantum homology, which is a variation of Floer theoretical constructs originally introduced by Oh, Vuglaris, and Woodward in 2019. Relative quantum homology comes equipped with a grading and ring structure, and for certain symplectic manifolds, it can be compared to differential forms through the use of a specific construction. Our study specifically examines how relative quantum homology responds to rational transformations of symplectic manifolds and provides a formula for its ring structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a particular type of Kähler manifolds known as toric varieties, this ring structure can be matched to the classical object, namely the ring formed by the polynomial functions divided by a specific ideal. This equivalence enables us to derive conclusions about the behavior of rational transformations, as well as providing an alternative proof of a previously established fact from mathematical literature. Additionally, our research introduces a novel complex, termed enhanced relative quantum homology, which contains both the original relative quantum homology and the Lagrangian chain invariant constructed from a specific rational transformation of the Gelfand-Dikii Hamiltonian system. This enhancement is crucial for demonstrating that the ring structure of the relative quantum homology is consistent with the algebraic structure of the Gelfand-Dikii Hamiltonian system, and it allows us to respond to a question initially posed by Oh, Vuglaris, and Woodward in 2019. Moreover, our results reveal that the ring structure of the relative quantum homology is preserved under a particular type of transformations known as Weyl group transformations, and it is also invariant under the action of a specific B-series known as Bruhat elements. This invariance is demonstrated by constructing a specific morphism, termed the Cassens operator, which acts on the ring structure of the relative quantum homology. Our research introduces the Cassens operator for the first time, and it is derived from the composition of two Hamiltonian operators, with the second being obtained from the Gelfand-Dikii Hamiltonian system through a process known as Hamiltonian reduction. The proposed safety evaluation was tested using a sample dataset comprising 20 symptom representations and 6 medical conditions, including pneumonia, lung cancer, bowel obstruction, spleen injury, liver injury, and kidney inflammation. The results were compared to those obtained using a straightforward metric based on classification accuracy. The research was published in the journal Nature Machine Intelligence. ViDaExpert is an application programmed in Java for visualizing and examining multidimensional data. The instrument presents data through nonlinear projections, enabling the integration of supplementary information via vectors. These vectors can be automatically determined by the application, using various methods, or they can be provided by the user. They serve to highlight specific aspects of the data, facilitate identification of patterns and groups, and provide more precise measurements of characteristics such as density and openness. The application includes a simple, user-friendly interface and is capable of handling massive datasets. It offers several processing algorithms, including Isomap, Local Dimensionality Reduction, and LEAP, and allows for in-depth analysis of data through its interactive 2D view and 3D viewer. The application caters to researchers and professionals in various fields including biology, medicine, finance, and social studies. It is particularly useful for the examination of high-dimensional genetic data, the study of complex networks, and the analysis of multidimensional time series data. The application is platform-independent and available for free use. The underlying methodology of ViDaExpert serves as a foundation for teaching purposes in statistics, biology, and computer science. The application is available for download on the website of the University of New South Wales. The version of the application reviewed in this paper is version 2.0.2.157.
